group: The session or access token is kept:

group: The session or access token is kept:

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: TanStack Query

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: SWR
lines: Read server data through SWR hooks with one key per resource and its parameters, revalidate with `mutate` after a write, and never copy the data into `useState` or fetch in an effect.

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: RTK Query
lines: Read and write server data through RTK Query endpoints in the existing API slices, invalidate with tags after a mutation, and never fetch in an effect or keep a copy of the answer in another slice.

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: Apollo Client (GraphQL)
lines: Read and write server data through Apollo Client hooks: ask only for the fields the screen shows, always select `id` so that the normalised cache can update, and update or refetch the affected queries after a mutation.

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: Relay (GraphQL)
lines: Read server data through Relay: each component declares the fields it needs in its own fragment, queries sit at the route, and the compiler output is regenerated, never edited by hand.

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: Plain `fetch`, no library

group: Server data is read and written through:
label: Something else
lines: Read and write server data through {value}, as the existing calls do; do not add another data-fetching library.

group: Every view that loads data shows its own loading, empty and error states.
lines: For every view that loads data, render the loading, empty, error and success states explicitly, with a way to retry after an error; never leave a blank area or an endless spinner, and keep showing the previous data while it refreshes.

group: Every view that loads data shows its own loading, empty and error states.
lines: Loading and errors are handled by the shared layout or boundary: do not add per-component loading or error states unasked.

group: After the user changes something, the interface:
label: Updates at once, and rolls back on failure
lines: Apply a mutation to the interface at once: snapshot the cached data, update it, roll back to the snapshot on failure with a visible message, then refetch so that the screen ends on the server state.

group: After the user changes something, the interface:
label: Waits for the answer of the server
lines: Do not update optimistically: disable the control and show progress while a mutation runs, then invalidate or refetch the data it changed, and show the server error on failure.

group: After the user changes something, the interface:
label: Depends on the action
lines: Update optimistically only for cheap, reversible actions (toggle, rename, reorder), with a rollback on failure; wait for the server for anything that creates, deletes, pays or changes rights.

group: Data that changes on the server reaches the screen by:
label: Refetching on action or on focus only
lines: There is no real-time channel: refresh data on user action, navigation or window focus, and do not add polling, Server-Sent Events or a WebSocket unasked.

group: Data that changes on the server reaches the screen by:
label: Polling
lines: Live data is polled: set the interval on the query rather than with a hand-written timer, stop while the tab is hidden or the component is unmounted, and do not add a push channel unasked.

group: Data that changes on the server reaches the screen by:
label: Server-Sent Events
lines: Live data arrives by Server-Sent Events: reuse the existing stream hook, close the `EventSource` on unmount, and use an event to invalidate or update the data cache rather than keeping a second copy in state.

group: Data that changes on the server reaches the screen by:
label: A WebSocket
lines: Live data arrives over a WebSocket: reuse the existing connection, reconnect with a growing delay, unsubscribe on unmount, and write messages into the data cache rather than a second copy in state.

group: Web Components (custom elements):
label: Are not used
lines: Do not introduce custom elements or Shadow DOM: build interface parts as components of the framework in use.

group: Web Components (custom elements):
label: Are used, from a library
lines: The app uses custom elements from a library: pass rich data as properties rather than attributes, listen to their custom events explicitly, and style them only through the parts and CSS variables they expose.

group: Web Components (custom elements):
label: Are written here, to share across frameworks
lines: Shared widgets are written as custom elements: give them a hyphenated prefixed name, keep markup and styles in Shadow DOM, expose attributes, properties, events, slots and CSS variables as the API, and depend on no framework inside.

group: The app registers a service worker:
label: No
lines: There is no service worker: do not add one, a web app manifest or offline caching unasked.

group: The app registers a service worker:
label: Yes, to install the app and cache its shell
lines: The service worker caches the application shell only: serve hashed assets cache-first and API calls from the network, never cache live data, and keep the update flow so that a new build replaces the old one instead of leaving clients on a stale bundle.

group: The app registers a service worker:
label: Yes, and the app works offline with its data
lines: The app works offline: read API data network-first with the cache as fallback, never cache-first, show when data is stale or the app is offline, and keep the update flow so that clients never stay on an old bundle.

group: Besides the browser, the front-end code also runs in:
label: A mobile shell (Capacitor, Ionic)
lines: The app also ships in a mobile web view shell: reach device features through the shell's plugins, behind a check that the platform has them, respect safe-area insets, and keep every screen usable by touch.

group: Besides the browser, the front-end code also runs in:
label: Electron
lines: The app also ships in Electron: keep Node access out of the renderer (context isolation on, `nodeIntegration` off), go through the preload bridge for anything native, and validate what crosses it.

group: Besides the browser, the front-end code also runs in:
label: Tauri
lines: The app also ships in Tauri: call native code only through its commands with the narrowest permissions, and avoid web features that the system web views do not all support.

group: Besides the browser, the front-end code also runs in:
label: A React Native app that shares its logic
lines: Logic is shared with a React Native app: keep shared modules free of DOM, `window` and CSS, and put anything that renders in the platform-specific code.

group: Besides the browser, the front-end code also runs in:
label: Nothing else
lines: The code runs in browsers only: do not add a mobile or desktop shell, and do not abstract browser APIs for another platform.

group: The front end is deployed as:
label: Static files on a CDN or a static host
lines: The front end ships as static files: nothing may need a server at runtime, and a client route must survive a reload through the host's rewrite of unknown paths to `index.html`; check that rewrite when routing changes.

group: The front end is deployed as:
label: A platform with serverless or edge functions
lines: The front end is deployed on a platform with serverless or edge functions: keep functions short and stateless, check that an API exists in that runtime before using a Node one, and keep configuration in the platform's environment settings.

group: The front end is deployed as:
label: Our own server or container
lines: The front end is served by the project's own server or container: change its configuration (rewrites, headers, runtime settings) in the repository, in the same change as the code that needs it.

group: The front end is deployed as:
label: Something else
lines: The front end is deployed with {value}: keep to what that host supports and do not add a second deployment target.

group: Each pull request gets its own preview deployment:
label: Yes
lines: Each pull request is deployed to its own preview URL: never hard-code the production origin or base path, and list in the pull request the screens and steps to check on the preview.

group: Each pull request gets its own preview deployment:
label: No
lines: There is no preview deployment: say in the pull request how to run the change locally and which screens to check.

group: The assistant checks a change to the interface in a real browser before handing back.
lines: After a change to the interface, run the app and check the changed screen in a browser before handing back: no error or warning in the console, the expected network requests, and the keyboard path; say what you checked.

group: The assistant checks a change to the interface in a real browser before handing back.
lines: Do not start the app or a browser to check a change: rely on types, lint and tests, and say what was not verified on screen.

group: The assistant checks that an API exists in the installed version before using it.
lines: Before using a library or browser API, check that it exists in the installed version (type definitions, package source or official documentation); never write a call from memory alone, and say what could not be verified.

group: The assistant checks that an API exists in the installed version before using it.
lines: Write library and browser API calls from what you know and let the type checker and the tests catch a wrong one; look an API up only when a check fails.

group: The API is:
label: REST
lines: The API is REST: model resources with plural nouns, use HTTP methods and status codes for what they mean, and keep the error body shape the same everywhere.

group: The API is:
label: GraphQL
lines: The API is GraphQL: extend the existing schema and resolvers; do not add REST endpoints next to it.

group: The API is:
label: RPC (tRPC, gRPC…)
lines: The API is RPC: add a typed procedure next to the existing ones; do not add REST endpoints next to it.

group: The API is:
label: Something else
lines: The API style is {value}; follow the existing endpoints and do not introduce another style.

group: A released endpoint never changes shape: a breaking change means a new version.
lines: Never rename, remove or retype a field of an existing endpoint; add an optional field or a new version instead.

group: A released endpoint never changes shape: a breaking change means a new version.
lines: An endpoint may change shape when every caller is updated in the same change.

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:
label: Zod

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:
label: VineJS

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:
label: Joi

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:
label: class-validator

group: Request inputs are validated at the boundary with:
label: Something else

group: Errors are handled:
label: By throwing typed errors that one central handler turns into responses
lines: Throw the project’s typed errors and let the central error handler build the response; do not catch an error only to answer from a route handler.

group: Errors are handled:
label: By returning result values, without throwing
lines: Return expected failures as result values and handle both cases at the call site; throw only for programming errors.

group: Errors are handled:
label: In each route handler
lines: Handle errors in the route handler that can answer them, with the same error body shape as the other handlers.

group: The code logs with:
label: A structured logger (pino, winston…)
lines: Log through the project’s logger, with a message and structured fields; never leave a `console.log` in the code.

group: The code logs with:
label: `console`
lines: Log with `console`; do not add a logging library.

group: Logs never contain secrets, tokens or personal data, even while debugging.
lines: Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, request bodies or personal data, at any level; log identifiers instead.

group: Logs never contain secrets, tokens or personal data, even while debugging.
lines: Request payloads may be logged at debug level in development; never log credentials or tokens.

group: The database is reached through:
label: An ORM
lines: Read and write the database through the project’s ORM models; drop to raw SQL only when the ORM cannot express the query, and say so.

group: The database is reached through:
label: A query builder
lines: Write queries with the project’s query builder; do not add an ORM.

group: The database is reached through:
label: Hand-written SQL
lines: Write SQL by hand, always with bound parameters; do not add an ORM or a query builder.

group: When a change needs a new table or column, the assistant:
label: Writes the migration
lines: Change the schema only through a new migration file; never edit a migration that has already run, and never run migrations against a shared database.

group: When a change needs a new table or column, the assistant:
label: Asks me first
lines: Ask before any schema change; once agreed, write a new migration file and never edit one that has already run.

group: When a change needs a new table or column, the assistant:
label: Never touches the schema
lines: Do not change the database schema or write migrations; describe the change that is needed and stop.

group: Database queries stay out of route handlers and controllers.
lines: Keep database queries in services or repositories; a route handler or controller never queries the database itself.

group: Database queries stay out of route handlers and controllers.
lines: A route handler may query the database directly for a simple read or write; do not add a layer only to wrap one query.

group: Outbound HTTP calls are made with:
label: A shared client of the project (timeouts, retries, headers)
lines: Make outbound HTTP calls through the project’s shared client, which sets timeouts, keep-alive and headers; never call `fetch` or build another client next to it.

group: Outbound HTTP calls are made with:
label: The built-in `fetch`
lines: Make outbound HTTP calls with the built-in `fetch`, each with `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, and check `response.ok` before reading the body; do not add an HTTP client library.

group: Outbound HTTP calls are made with:
label: Another library
lines: Make outbound HTTP calls with {value}, as the existing calls do; do not add another HTTP client.

group: In production, the Node.js process is:
label: Behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that ends TLS
lines: A reverse proxy ends TLS in front of the app: listen on plain HTTP, read the client address and scheme through the framework’s trusted-proxy setting, never from `X-Forwarded-*` headers by hand, and leave TLS, compression and static files to the proxy.

group: In production, the Node.js process is:
label: Exposed directly, and ends TLS itself
lines: The process is exposed directly: it ends TLS itself, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, sends `Strict-Transport-Security`, and never trusts `X-Forwarded-*` headers.

group: The API answers with the precise status code, never 200 or 400 for everything.
lines: Answer with the precise status: 201 for a creation, 204 for an empty success, 401 when the caller is not authenticated, 403 when authenticated but not allowed, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict; never 200 with an error in the body.

group: The API answers with the precise status code, never 200 or 400 for everything.
lines: Keep to the status codes the existing endpoints already return; do not introduce a new one without asking.

group: A write that a client may retry is made safe by:
label: An `Idempotency-Key` header on POST
lines: A POST that creates or charges something accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header: store the key with the result, and answer a repeated key with the first result instead of doing the work twice.

group: A write that a client may retry is made safe by:
label: Idempotent methods and unique constraints only (PUT, DELETE, upsert)
lines: Make retried writes safe by design: PUT replaces and DELETE removes, so repeating them leaves the same state; give a creation a client-chosen id or a unique constraint rather than a store of idempotency keys.

group: A write that a client may retry is made safe by:
label: Nothing: a retry may repeat the effect
lines: Writes are not protected against retries: do not add an idempotency mechanism unasked, but say when a new POST would be harmful to repeat.

group: CPU-heavy work (image processing, large parsing, bulk hashing) runs:
label: In worker threads
lines: Run CPU-heavy work in the project’s worker threads, never on the event loop: no synchronous loop over large data, and no `*Sync` call from `fs`, `crypto` or `zlib` in a request handler.

group: CPU-heavy work (image processing, large parsing, bulk hashing) runs:
label: In a background job, outside the API process
lines: Hand CPU-heavy work to a background job: the API process never runs it on the event loop, and never calls a `*Sync` function of `fs`, `crypto` or `zlib` in a request handler.

group: CPU-heavy work (image processing, large parsing, bulk hashing) runs:
label: In another service
lines: CPU-heavy work belongs to the service built for it: call that service from the API, and never run such work on the event loop here.

group: CPU-heavy work (image processing, large parsing, bulk hashing) runs:
label: Nowhere: the API only does I/O
lines: The API only does I/O: when a change would add CPU-heavy work to a request, stop and say so instead of running it on the event loop.

group: CI and production install exactly what the committed lockfile says.
lines: Commit the lockfile with every dependency change, and install with the frozen-lockfile command (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) in CI and images; never delete or regenerate the lockfile to make an install pass.

group: CI and production install exactly what the committed lockfile says.
lines: The lockfile may be regenerated when an install fails; say so, and list the versions that moved.

group: The code runs as:
label: ES modules
lines: The code runs as ES modules: use `import` and `export`, and `import.meta` in place of `__dirname`; never add `require` or `module.exports`.

group: The code runs as:
label: CommonJS
lines: The code runs as CommonJS: keep the existing import style, load an ESM-only package with a dynamic `import()`, do not use top-level `await`, and do not convert the project to ES modules unasked.

group: A write that touches several rows or tables always runs in one transaction.
lines: Wrap every operation that writes more than one row or table in one transaction, through the project’s transaction helper; keep it short, and never await an HTTP call or any other slow outside call inside it.

group: A write that touches several rows or tables always runs in one transaction.
lines: Use a transaction only where a partial write would leave wrong data; do not wrap single statements or reads.

group: When two requests may change the same row (stock, balance, quota), the code uses:
label: One conditional `UPDATE` (`… WHERE available > 0`)
lines: Never read a value and write it back: change it in one conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE` that states the condition, and treat zero affected rows as the refusal.

group: When two requests may change the same row (stock, balance, quota), the code uses:
label: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in a transaction
lines: Before changing a row from a value read earlier, lock it with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in the same transaction; always lock rows in the same order to avoid deadlocks.

group: When two requests may change the same row (stock, balance, quota), the code uses:
label: A version column (optimistic locking)
lines: Guard concurrent changes with the version column: update `WHERE version = <the one read>`, increment it, and answer a conflict (409) when no row was changed.

group: When two requests may change the same row (stock, balance, quota), the code uses:
label: Something else
lines: Guard concurrent changes to the same row with {value}; never read a value and write it back unguarded.

group: In database code, the assistant always:
label: Avoids one query per item (N+1)
lines: Never query inside a loop: load related rows with a join, an eager load or one `IN (...)` query (a batching loader in GraphQL resolvers), and check the SQL that an ORM call generates.

group: In database code, the assistant always:
label: Selects only the columns it needs, with a limit
lines: Select the columns the code uses, never `SELECT *` on a wide table, and bound every list query with a limit.

group: In database code, the assistant always:
label: Adds the index a new query needs
lines: When a new query filters, joins or sorts on a column of a table that can grow, add the matching index in the same change, and index every foreign key; do not add an index that no query uses.

group: In database code, the assistant always:
label: Enforces integrity with constraints in the schema
lines: Enforce integrity in the schema, not only in code: `NOT NULL`, unique, foreign key and check constraints; store each fact once, and denormalize only where a measurement justifies it.

group: In database code, the assistant always:
label: Writes migrations that run without blocking a live table
lines: Write migrations that run on a live database next to the previous code: create an index with `CONCURRENTLY`, add a column as nullable then backfill in batches, and drop a column one release after the code stops using it.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: A key-value store (Redis, DynamoDB…)
lines: The key-value store holds data read by key only (sessions, counters, quotas): name keys with the existing prefixes, set an expiry on anything temporary, and never scan keys (`KEYS`) in application code.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: A document database (MongoDB…)
lines: Model documents after the queries that read them: embed what is read together, do not spread one aggregate over collections joined by id in code, and validate a document’s shape when writing it.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: A search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch…)
lines: The search engine is a copy, never the source of truth: write to the main database first, update the index from a job or an event, and keep reindexing from the database possible.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: A time series database (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB…)
lines: Timestamped measurements go to the time series store: append, never update in place, always query with a time range, and rely on its retention rules to delete old data.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: An analytical database (ClickHouse…)
lines: Aggregates over large volumes run on the analytical database, fed by batches of inserts: never run such a query on the transactional database from a request, and never write single rows or transactions to the analytical one.

group: Besides the main database, the project stores data in:
label: Nothing else
lines: The main database is the only store: do not introduce another database, a cache or a search engine unasked; first show the access pattern that the main database cannot serve.

group: I prefer typed columns and tables to JSON columns.
lines: Model data with typed columns and tables; use a JSON column only for data that is stored and returned whole, never filtered, joined or constrained.

group: I prefer typed columns and tables to JSON columns.
lines: A JSON column is fine for data whose shape varies; validate its shape with a schema when writing it, and index the keys that are queried.

group: Reads go to:
label: The primary only
lines: There is one database connection for reads and writes: do not add read/write splitting unasked.

group: Reads go to:
label: Read replicas, when a little lag is acceptable
lines: Send only reads that tolerate lag to the read replica connection; read from the primary inside a transaction and right after a write, so that a user always sees what they just changed.

group: Large tables are:
label: Neither partitioned nor sharded
lines: Tables are neither partitioned nor sharded: do not introduce either unasked; propose it with the table size and the query that needs it.

group: Large tables are:
label: Partitioned (by date, by tenant…)
lines: Some tables are partitioned: always filter on the partition key so that only the needed partitions are read, and remove old data by dropping a partition, never with a bulk `DELETE`.

group: Large tables are:
label: Sharded across several databases
lines: Data is sharded: every query carries the shard key, no join or transaction crosses shards, a row’s shard key never changes, and a new table states its shard key before any code is written.

group: Every query goes through one shared connection pool.
lines: Take database connections from the shared pool only and release them on every path (`finally`, or the ORM’s own handling); never open a connection per request, hold one across a slow call, or raise the pool size to hide a slow query.

group: Every query goes through one shared connection pool.
lines: Connection handling is left to the platform (serverless driver, external pooler): do not add a pool or change connection settings unasked.

group: List endpoints are paginated with:
label: A page number and a page size
lines: Paginate every list endpoint with a page number and a page size, with a default and a maximum page size, a stable sort order, and the same response envelope as the existing lists.

group: List endpoints are paginated with:
label: A cursor (keyset)
lines: Paginate every list endpoint with an opaque cursor over a unique, indexed sort key (keyset), with a maximum page size; never use `OFFSET` on a table that grows.

group: List endpoints are paginated with:
label: Nothing: lists are returned whole
lines: Lists are returned whole: do not add pagination unasked, but say when a new list has no upper bound.

group: The API version is carried by:
label: The URL (`/v1/…`)
lines: Put every new route under the current version prefix (`/v1/...`); a breaking change goes under a new prefix, and the old one keeps working until its removal is announced.

group: The API version is carried by:
label: A header or a media type
lines: The API version comes from a request header: read it through the existing helper, treat a missing one as the existing routes do, and never put a version in a URL.

group: The API version is carried by:
label: Nothing: there is one version
lines: The API has one version: do not add a version prefix or header unasked.

group: The API is described by:
label: An OpenAPI (or schema) file written before the code
lines: The API description is written first: change the OpenAPI or schema file before the code, then make the code match it, with every status code and error shape the endpoint can return.

group: The API is described by:
label: A description generated from the code
lines: The API description is generated from the code: keep the route schemas and types it reads complete, regenerate it with the project’s command after any change to a route, and never edit the generated file by hand.

group: The API is described by:
label: No formal description
lines: There is no formal API description: do not add one unasked; document a new or changed endpoint where the existing ones are documented.

group: Callers are authenticated with:
label: A server-side session behind a cookie
lines: Sessions live on the server behind a cookie set `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` or stricter: never put a session id or a token in `localStorage` or a URL, renew the session id at login, and protect state-changing routes against CSRF.

group: Callers are authenticated with:
label: JWT access tokens
lines: Access tokens are JWTs: verify signature, expected algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry on every request with the project’s helper, keep their lifetime short (5 to 15 minutes) next to a revocable refresh token, and never put a secret in the payload.

group: Callers are authenticated with:
label: Opaque tokens or API keys
lines: Callers send an opaque token in `Authorization: Bearer`: store only its hash, show the value once at creation, give each token scopes and an expiry, and never accept one from a query string.

group: Callers are authenticated with:
label: An external identity provider (OpenID Connect, SAML)
lines: Sign-in is delegated to an identity provider: use the authorization code flow with PKCE, validate `state` and the ID token (signature, issuer, audience, expiry), take the identity from the ID token, and never add a password login next to it.

group: Callers are authenticated with:
label: Something else
lines: Callers are authenticated with {value}: reuse the existing mechanism, and never add a second one next to it.

group: Every route checks, on the server, that the caller may act on that exact resource.
lines: On every route that reads or changes a resource, check through the project’s authorization helper that it belongs to the caller; never trust an id from the URL or the body, and add a test that tries another user’s resource.

group: Every route checks, on the server, that the caller may act on that exact resource.
lines: Access is checked by a layer above the handlers (gateway, global guard): do not repeat the check in each handler, but say when a new route is not covered by it.

group: Passwords are hashed with:
label: Argon2id
lines: Hash passwords with Argon2id through the project’s helper, with a salt per password and a cost tuned to about 100 to 300 ms; never use MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 for a password, even salted.

group: Passwords are hashed with:
label: bcrypt
lines: Hash passwords with bcrypt through the project’s helper; bcrypt ignores what comes after 72 bytes, so cap the accepted length, and never use MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 for a password, even salted.

group: Passwords are hashed with:
label: scrypt
lines: Hash passwords with scrypt through the project’s helper, with a salt per password; never use MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 for a password, even salted.

group: Passwords are hashed with:
label: Nothing: the application stores no password
lines: The application stores no password: never add a password column, a password login or a reset flow; sign-in stays with the existing provider.

group: Cross-origin requests from browsers (CORS) are:
label: Allowed for a list of known origins
lines: CORS allows the origins of the configured list only: add an origin to that list, never answer `*` or reflect the `Origin` header, and never combine a wildcard with credentials.

group: Cross-origin requests from browsers (CORS) are:
label: Not allowed: the front end is on the same origin
lines: The API sends no CORS headers because the front end is on the same origin: do not enable CORS to make a call pass.

group: Cross-origin requests from browsers (CORS) are:
label: Allowed for any origin, without credentials (public API)
lines: CORS is open to any origin because the API is public: keep it without credentials (no cookies), and authenticate with a token in a header.

group: Security headers (HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options`…) are set by:
label: The application (helmet or the framework’s equivalent)
lines: Security headers are set in one place in the application (HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, frame and content security policies): change them there, never per route, and never loosen a policy (`unsafe-inline`, `*`) without asking.

group: Security headers (HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options`…) are set by:
label: The reverse proxy or the CDN
lines: Security headers are set by the reverse proxy or the CDN: do not set them again in application code; when a change needs a header or a looser policy, say which one and where.

group: Security headers (HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options`…) are set by:
label: Nobody yet
lines: No security headers are set yet: do not add a library for them unasked, but say so when a change serves HTML or sets a cookie.

group: The back end also:
label: Renders HTML or emails that contain user content
lines: Escape user content by default wherever it reaches HTML or an email, through the template engine’s auto-escaping; never build markup by string concatenation, and never mark user content as safe.

group: The back end also:
label: Fetches URLs given by users (webhooks, imports, previews)
lines: Before fetching a URL given by a user, allow only `http` and `https`, resolve the host and refuse private, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses, do not follow redirects unchecked, and set a timeout and a size limit.

group: The back end also:
label: Accepts file uploads
lines: For an upload, check type and size at the boundary, never trust the client’s file name or content type, store it outside the web root under a generated name, and serve it back with an explicit `Content-Type`.

group: The back end also:
label: Runs commands or opens paths built from input
lines: Never pass input to a shell: use `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and no `shell` option, and resolve any path built from input against a fixed base folder, refusing what escapes it.

group: The back end also:
label: None of these
lines: The back end renders no HTML, fetches no user-given URL, takes no upload and runs no command: when a change would start doing one of these, say so first.

group: GET responses state how they may be cached (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`).
lines: Set `Cache-Control` on every GET response: `public, max-age` only when the answer is the same for every caller, `private` or `no-store` for anything tied to a user or a token, and an `ETag` answered with 304 where clients revalidate.

group: GET responses state how they may be cached (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`).
lines: Do not add caching headers or ETags unasked: responses are not meant to be cached by clients or by a CDN.

group: On the server, computed or fetched data is cached in:
label: A shared cache (Redis, Memcached…)
lines: Cache through the project’s cache helper on the shared store: a namespaced key that includes everything the value depends on (tenant, user, locale, version), a TTL on every entry, and a working path when the cache is down.

group: On the server, computed or fetched data is cached in:
label: The memory of each process
lines: Cache in process memory only small, nearly static data, with a size bound and a TTL: each instance has its own copy, so never cache there what must be the same on every instance.

group: On the server, computed or fetched data is cached in:
label: Nothing
lines: There is no server-side cache: do not add one unasked; fix the slow query or call first, and propose a cache together with its invalidation rule.

group: A cached value is refreshed by:
label: Expiry only (TTL)
lines: Cached values expire by TTL only: choose the TTL from how stale the value may be, add 10 to 20 % of random jitter so that keys do not expire together, and never cache what must be exact (permissions, balances).

group: A cached value is refreshed by:
label: Deleting the key when the data is written
lines: Delete the cache key in the code path that writes the data, after the write is committed, and keep a TTL as a safety net; a new cached read comes with the list of writes that purge it.

group: A cached value is refreshed by:
label: A version in the key
lines: Put the data’s version in the cache key and bump it on write, so that stale entries are never read and simply expire; keep a TTL on every entry.

group: The service is built into a container image:
label: From a Dockerfile in this repository
lines: Keep the Dockerfile multi-stage, on a base image pinned to an exact version: install from the lockfile, copy only the build output and production dependencies into the last stage, run as a non-root user, and keep secrets out of every layer.
Run one process per container, and do not let Node.js be PID 1 without an init process (`--init`, tini): it must receive `SIGTERM` and reap child processes.

group: The service is built into a container image:
label: No: the platform builds or runs it
lines: No container image is built here: do not add a Dockerfile or a Compose file unasked.

group: All configuration comes from environment variables, validated at startup.
lines: Read configuration from environment variables only, through the one module that validates them at startup; never read `process.env` elsewhere, never hard-code a URL, a port or a credential, and add each new variable to the example env file.

group: All configuration comes from environment variables, validated at startup.
lines: Configuration lives in the project’s configuration files: follow them, and do not move settings to environment variables unasked.

group: On `SIGTERM`, the process finishes what is in flight before it exits.
lines: Keep shutdown clean: on `SIGTERM`, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests and jobs within the grace period, then close pools and exit; register every new long-lived resource (server, worker, timer, connection) in that shutdown path.

group: On `SIGTERM`, the process finishes what is in flight before it exits.
lines: Do not add signal handling: the process may be stopped at any time, so keep every operation safe to interrupt and to run again.

group: The back end is:
label: One application (a modular monolith)
lines: The back end is one modular monolith: add code to the module that owns the domain, call another module only through its public interface, and never propose a new service or a message bus for what a function call does.

group: The back end is:
label: Several services, each with its own data
lines: Each service owns its data: never read or write another service’s tables, go through its API or its events, treat every such call as able to fail or time out, and do not add a new service unasked.

group: The back end is:
label: Functions run on demand (serverless)
lines: Code runs as short-lived functions: keep startup light, create clients outside the handler, hold no state in memory between invocations, and hand to a queue any work that may pass the time limit.

group: A process keeps nothing in memory or on its disk that another instance would need.
lines: Keep processes stateless: no session, counter, lock, scheduled timer or uploaded file in process memory or on the local disk that another instance would need; put shared state in the database, the shared cache or object storage.

group: A process keeps nothing in memory or on its disk that another instance would need.
lines: A single instance runs, so state in process memory is acceptable; mark it with a comment so that it can be moved when a second instance is added.

group: Work that does not fit in a request runs on:
label: A job queue (BullMQ, pg-boss…)
lines: Slow work runs on the job queue: enqueue from the request with a small payload of ids, make each handler safe to run twice, set a number of attempts with backoff, and never do slow work in the request itself.

group: Work that does not fit in a request runs on:
label: A message broker (RabbitMQ, SQS…)
lines: Work goes through the message broker: acknowledge a message only after its work is committed, make every consumer safe to run twice, and send repeated failures to a dead-letter queue instead of requeueing forever.

group: Work that does not fit in a request runs on:
label: An event log (Kafka…)
lines: Events go through a partitioned log: pick the key whose events must stay ordered, since order holds within a partition only, make consumers safe to replay, and change an event’s schema by adding fields only.

group: Work that does not fit in a request runs on:
label: Nothing: everything runs in the request
lines: There is no queue: do not add a broker or a job library unasked; keep work in the request short, and say when a change needs work that cannot fit in it.

group: Work that does not fit in a request runs on:
label: Something else
lines: Work outside the request runs on {value}: follow the existing producers and consumers, and make every handler safe to run twice.

group: Updates are pushed to clients with:
label: Server-Sent Events
lines: Push updates with Server-Sent Events: send an `id` with each event so that a client resumes with `Last-Event-ID`, send a heartbeat comment, free the listener when the connection closes, and do not add WebSockets for a one-way stream.

group: Updates are pushed to clients with:
label: WebSockets
lines: Push updates over the existing WebSocket layer: authenticate at the handshake, validate every incoming message, free listeners on close, and publish through the shared channel, not process memory, so that every instance reaches its clients.

group: Updates are pushed to clients with:
label: Polling by the client
lines: Clients poll for updates: keep the polled endpoint cheap (an ETag and 304, or a `since` parameter), and do not add Server-Sent Events or WebSockets unasked.

group: Updates are pushed to clients with:
label: Nothing: there is no live update
lines: There is no live update channel: do not add Server-Sent Events, WebSockets or polling unasked.

group: Webhooks: the back end
label: Sends some to its users
lines: Send a webhook from a background job, never inside the request: sign the payload, retry with backoff, and include an event id so that the receiver can ignore a duplicate.

group: Webhooks: the back end
label: Receives some from other services
lines: On an incoming webhook, verify the signature over the raw body before parsing it, answer 2xx fast and do the work in a job, and ignore an event id that was already handled.

group: Webhooks: the back end
label: Neither sends nor receives any
lines: The back end neither sends nor receives webhooks: do not add any unasked.

group: Request rates are limited:
label: In the application, with a shared counter
lines: Rate limits live in the application, with counters in the shared store, never in process memory: put every new public or costly route (sign-in, password reset, search, export) behind the limiter, keyed by account or by IP, and answer 429 with `Retry-After`.

group: Request rates are limited:
label: At the reverse proxy or the API gateway
lines: Rate limits are set at the reverse proxy or the gateway: do not add a limiter in application code; say when a new route is costly or sensitive enough to need its own limit there.

group: Request rates are limited:
label: Nowhere
lines: No rate limit exists: do not add a limiter unasked, but say when a new route (sign-in, password reset, costly query) is open to abuse without one.

group: Under load, or when a dependency fails, the code:
label: Retries with backoff, idempotent calls only
lines: Retry a failed call to a dependency only when it is idempotent, with exponential backoff, jitter and a small cap on attempts; honor `Retry-After`, and never retry a 4xx other than 429.

group: Under load, or when a dependency fails, the code:
label: Cuts calls to a failing dependency (circuit breaker)
lines: Call unreliable dependencies through the project’s circuit breaker, with a short timeout, so that a slow dependency fails fast instead of holding connections; do not write a second breaker.

group: Under load, or when a dependency fails, the code:
label: Bounds queues and concurrency, and refuses the rest
lines: Bound everything that can pile up: a maximum length on queues and buffers, a concurrency limit on parallel work (no unbounded `Promise.all` over input-sized lists), a request body limit, and a 429 or 503 with `Retry-After` when full.

group: Under load, or when a dependency fails, the code:
label: Serves a degraded answer rather than an error
lines: When a secondary dependency fails, keep the main path working: serve the cached or partial answer and mark it as such, and never let an optional feature fail the whole request.

group: A performance change starts from a measurement, never from intuition.
lines: Do not optimise by intuition: measure first (CPU profile, event loop lag, query plan, p99 latency rather than the average), change one thing, and report the numbers before and after.

group: A performance change starts from a measurement, never from intuition.
lines: Write the faster version directly when the cost is obvious; a measurement is only needed before a change that makes the code harder to read.

group: Tests that touch the database run against:
label: A real database (container or test instance)
lines: Test database code against the real test database, never a mock: run the migrations, isolate each test (transaction rollback or truncation), and create the rows a test needs in the test itself.

group: Tests that touch the database run against:
label: An in-memory substitute (SQLite, pg-mem…)
lines: Tests run on an in-memory substitute of the database: keep queries within what it supports, and say when a query uses a feature only the real database has, since the tests cannot prove it.

group: Tests that touch the database run against:
label: Mocks of the data layer
lines: Tests mock the data layer: mock at the repository or service boundary, never the driver, and say that SQL and migrations are not covered when a change touches them.

group: Every new endpoint comes with a test that calls it over HTTP.
lines: Give every new or changed endpoint a test that calls it over HTTP: the success case, an invalid input, a call without credentials and a call on another user’s resource, each checking the status code and the body.

group: Every new endpoint comes with a test that calls it over HTTP.
lines: Test the services and business rules directly, in fast tests without network; do not add HTTP-level tests unasked.

group: The service emits:
label: Metrics
lines: Instrument new endpoints, jobs and outbound calls with the existing metrics helpers (count, errors, duration as a histogram), and keep label values few and bounded: never a user id, an email or a raw URL as a label.

group: The service emits:
label: Traces (OpenTelemetry…)
lines: Let the existing tracing setup create spans: add one only around a significant unit of work, pass the context through queues and outbound calls, and never put a secret or personal data in an attribute.

group: The service emits:
label: A request or trace id in every log line
lines: Carry the request or trace id through every log line, job payload and outbound call of a request, with the existing context helper rather than a parameter threaded by hand.

group: The service emits:
label: Health endpoints for the platform
lines: Keep the liveness endpoint free of dependencies and let the readiness endpoint check the ones a request needs: wire any new required dependency into readiness, and keep both cheap and unauthenticated.

group: The service emits:
label: None of these
lines: The service has no metrics, traces or health endpoints: do not add an observability library unasked.

group: A call to a language model from the back end runs:
label: In a background job; the client is told when it is done
lines: Call the model from a background job, never in a request handler: the request stores the task and answers at once, and the job saves the result and can be retried without repeating a side effect.

group: A call to a language model from the back end runs:
label: In the request, streamed to the client
lines: Call the model in the request and stream the answer to the client as it arrives: stop the provider call when the client disconnects, and save what must be kept only once the stream has ended.

group: A call to a language model from the back end runs:
label: In the request, the client waits for the whole answer
lines: The model is called in the request and the client waits: set a strict timeout and a small output limit, keep the call out of any database transaction, and say when a call may last long enough to need a job.

group: A call to a language model from the back end runs:
label: Nowhere: the back end calls no model
lines: The back end calls no language model: do not add a provider SDK or a model call unasked.

group: Around every call to a model, the code:
label: Goes through one client module, on the server
lines: Call the model provider through the project’s one client module, on the server only, with the key read from configuration: never call the provider from a handler directly, and never send the key to a client.

group: Around every call to a model, the code:
label: Sets a timeout, capped retries and a fallback
lines: Treat the model provider as a slow dependency that fails: a timeout on every call, retries with backoff on rate limits and 5xx only, capped, and a fallback or a clear error for the user.

group: Around every call to a model, the code:
label: Bounds and records token usage
lines: Cap the output tokens and the size of the context on every model call, record token usage per account or feature, reuse a cached answer for an identical request, and check the account’s limit before calling.

group: Around every call to a model, the code:
label: Treats the answer as untrusted input
lines: Treat a model’s answer as untrusted input: validate it against a schema before using it, never run a query, a command or a paid or destructive action from it without a server-side permission check, and escape it before display.

group: Each task is done:
label: In its own worktree, on its own branch
lines: Before the first edit, create a git worktree with its own branch from the up-to-date main branch, and work only there; never create or switch branches in the main checkout.

group: Each task is done:
label: On its own branch
lines: Before the first edit, create a branch from the up-to-date main branch; never work on the main branch itself.

group: Each task is done:
label: Directly on the main branch
lines: Work on the main branch; do not create a branch unless asked to.

group: Commit messages follow:
label: Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`…)
lines: Write commit messages as Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary` in the imperative, with the reason in the body when it is not obvious.

group: Commit messages follow:
label: A short imperative sentence, without prefix
lines: Write the commit subject as a short imperative sentence without a prefix, with the reason in the body when it is not obvious.

group: Commit messages follow:
label: Another convention
lines: Commit messages follow this convention: {value}.

group: On its own, the assistant may:
label: Neither commit nor push
lines: Never commit or push unless asked to; leave the changes in the working tree and summarize them.

group: On its own, the assistant may:
label: Commit, but not push
lines: Commit finished work in coherent commits; never push unless asked to.

group: On its own, the assistant may:
label: Commit and push its branch
lines: Commit finished work in coherent commits and push the task’s branch; never push to the main branch and never merge.

group: A pull request stays reviewable up to about:
label: 200 changed lines
lines: Keep a pull request under about 200 changed lines, generated files aside; past that, propose how to split it before going on.

group: A pull request stays reviewable up to about:
label: 400 changed lines
lines: Keep a pull request under about 400 changed lines, generated files aside; past that, propose how to split it before going on.

group: A pull request stays reviewable up to about:
label: 800 changed lines
lines: Keep a pull request under about 800 changed lines, generated files aside; past that, propose how to split it before going on.

group: A pull request stays reviewable up to about:
label: No limit
lines: A pull request has no size limit, but covers one subject: leave unrelated fixes for another one.

group: Never committed:
label: Secrets and `.env` files
lines: Never commit a secret, a key, a token or a `.env` file; if one is staged, unstage it and say so.

group: Never committed:
label: Build output and generated files
lines: Never commit build output or generated files that the repository ignores or rebuilds.

group: Never committed:
label: Large binary files
lines: Never commit a large binary file; ask where it should live instead.

group: Never committed:
label: Debug statements and commented-out code
lines: Never commit debug statements, temporary files or commented-out code.

group: Never committed:
label: Changes unrelated to the task (formatting, lockfile churn)
lines: Never commit changes unrelated to the task: no reformatting of untouched code, no lockfile change without a dependency change.

group: Pushed history is never rewritten: no amend, no rebase, no force-push.
lines: Never rewrite pushed history: no amend, rebase or force-push; fix with a new commit.

group: Pushed history is never rewritten: no amend, no rebase, no force-push.
lines: Tidy a task’s branch with amend or rebase before review when it helps; never rewrite the main branch.

group: Commits and pull requests never mention the assistant.
lines: Never credit a coding assistant in a commit, a pull request or a comment: no co-author trailer, no "generated with" footer.

group: Commits and pull requests never mention the assistant.
lines: Add a co-author trailer naming the assistant to every commit it writes.

group: Every pull request is checked in CI:
label: By a generated GitHub Actions workflow (adds `.github/workflows/agent-conventions.yml`)
lines: The `.github/workflows/agent-conventions.yml` workflow runs the checks on every pull request: never edit, skip or disable it; fix what it reports.

group: The assistant never reads or prints secrets (`.env` files, keys, tokens).
lines: Never open, print or copy a secret (`.env` files, keys, tokens); name a secret by its variable, read `.env.example` instead, and never hard-code one.

group: The assistant never reads or prints secrets (`.env` files, keys, tokens).
lines: Reading local `.env` files is allowed to debug configuration; never repeat a secret value in an answer, a log or a file, and never hard-code one.

group: To add a dependency, the assistant:
label: Asks me first
lines: Ask before adding a dependency: say what it is for, who maintains it and what was considered instead.

group: To add a dependency, the assistant:
label: Decides, and tells me
lines: Add a dependency only when it clearly beats writing the code; pick a maintained, widely used package and say what was added.

group: To add a dependency, the assistant:
label: Never adds one
lines: Never add a dependency: solve the task with what the project already has, or stop and say what is missing.

group: Versions of packages and tools are written as:
label: Exact versions
lines: Pin every package, tool and base image to an exact version: never `latest`, `^`, `~` or another range.

group: Versions of packages and tools are written as:
label: Ranges (`^`, `~`)
lines: Write versions with the ranges the project already uses; never `latest`, and do not pin or loosen existing ones as a side effect.

group: Anything that comes from outside the program is untrusted until validated, internal services and files included.
lines: Treat every value from outside the program as untrusted (requests, files, environment, other services): validate it where it enters, and never build SQL, a shell command or HTML by concatenating it.

group: Anything that comes from outside the program is untrusted until validated, internal services and files included.
lines: Validate what users and third parties send; data from the project’s own services and files can be used as is. Never build SQL, a shell command or HTML by concatenating a user value.

group: Commands that delete or overwrite (`rm -rf`, dropping a table, `git reset --hard`, force-push):
label: The assistant never runs them
lines: Never run a command that deletes or overwrites work or data (`rm -rf`, dropping a table or a database, `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, force-push); give the command and what it removes instead.

group: Commands that delete or overwrite (`rm -rf`, dropping a table, `git reset --hard`, force-push):
label: The assistant asks me first
lines: Ask before any command that deletes or overwrites work or data (`rm -rf`, dropping a table or a database, `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, force-push), and say what it will remove.

group: Commands that delete or overwrite (`rm -rf`, dropping a table, `git reset --hard`, force-push):
label: Allowed inside the working directory and local databases
lines: Commands that delete or overwrite are allowed only inside the working directory and on local development databases; never outside it, on a shared environment or on uncommitted work that is not yours.

group: The assistant may reach the network:
label: Never
lines: Do not use the network: no download, no call to an external service; ask when one is needed.

group: The assistant may reach the network:
label: For the package registry and official documentation only
lines: Use the network only for the package registry and official documentation; ask before reaching anything else.

group: The assistant may reach the network:
label: Freely
lines: Network access is allowed for reading; never send project code, data or secrets to an external service, and never run a script straight from a URL.

group: The assistant asks me before changing authentication, permissions or cryptography code.
lines: Ask before changing authentication, authorization, session or cryptography code, never weaken a check to make a test pass, and never write your own cryptography.

group: The assistant asks me before changing authentication, permissions or cryptography code.
lines: Change authentication and authorization code like any other, with a test for the allowed case and one for the refused case; never write your own cryptography.

group: The assistant runs:
label: In a sandboxed development container, behind a firewall (adds a `.devcontainer` folder)
lines: You run inside a development container whose firewall only lets through the hosts listed in `.devcontainer/init-firewall.sh`: never try to change, stop or get around the firewall, and never edit the `.devcontainer` folder; when a host you need is blocked, stop and ask.

group: The assistant runs:
label: Directly on my machine
lines: You run directly on the developer’s machine, with no sandbox around you: never read or change anything outside the working directory.

group: Before designing anything, the assistant writes down the requirements and the scale it works from.
lines: Before proposing a design, write down what the feature must do, what is out of scope, the load at peak, the read/write ratio, and the consistency, latency and availability it needs; ask for what is missing instead of guessing.

group: Before designing anything, the assistant writes down the requirements and the scale it works from.
lines: Start from a concrete design proposal and list the assumptions behind it in a few lines; do not open with a round of questions.

group: A design proposal names the option it set aside and what the chosen one costs.
lines: For every design decision, name at least one option that was set aside and why, what the chosen one costs, and the bottleneck or single point of failure that remains.

group: A design proposal names the option it set aside and what the chosen one costs.
lines: Propose one design and keep the reasoning short; compare alternatives only when asked.

group: The system is sized for:
label: A small load (an internal tool, a few requests per second)
lines: The load is small: prefer the simplest design that works on one database and a few instances; do not add a cache, a queue, replicas or sharding for scale unless asked.

group: The system is sized for:
label: Tens to hundreds of requests per second
lines: The load is tens to hundreds of requests per second: size a new feature for the peak (3 to 10 times the average), keep every query indexed and paginated, and do not add sharding or a new data store unless asked.

group: The system is sized for:
label: Thousands of requests per second or more
lines: The load is thousands of requests per second: estimate the requests per second, the read/write ratio and the storage a new feature adds before writing it, size for the peak (3 to 10 times the average), and say which component saturates first.

group: The application scales by:
label: Adding stateless instances behind a load balancer
lines: Several identical instances serve requests: keep no state in process memory or on local disk between two requests (sessions, counters, locks, uploads, timers); put it in the database, the shared cache or object storage.
When a change adds load to the application instances, say how the data layer follows: adding instances only moves the bottleneck to a single database.

group: The application scales by:
label: Running one instance on a bigger machine
lines: One instance runs the application: do not add a load balancer, clustering or distributed locks unless asked, and say so when a change keeps state in memory that a second instance would not share.

group: The application scales by:
label: Running short-lived functions (serverless)
lines: The code runs in short-lived functions: keep nothing in memory or on disk between invocations, create clients and connections once outside the handler, and keep start-up work small.

group: The application scales by:
label: Something else
lines: The application scales by {value}; respect that model and do not introduce another one.

group: State kept between two requests of a user (session, cart, progress) lives in:
label: A shared store (Redis, Memcached)
lines: Per-user state between requests lives in the shared store: read and write it there with an expiry, never in a module-level variable or an in-process map.

group: State kept between two requests of a user (session, cart, progress) lives in:
label: The database
lines: Per-user state between requests lives in the database: never keep it in process memory, and do not add a second store for it.

group: State kept between two requests of a user (session, cart, progress) lives in:
label: The client (signed token or cookie)
lines: Per-user state travels with the client in a signed token or cookie: keep it small, verify the signature before trusting it, never store a secret in it, and keep no server-side copy in memory.

group: State kept between two requests of a user (session, cart, progress) lives in:
label: The memory of the instance, with sticky sessions
lines: Sessions live in instance memory behind sticky sessions: a restart loses them, so never keep there anything a user cannot lose, and do not make more features depend on the affinity.

group: Latency is read as percentiles (p50, p95, p99), never as an average alone.
lines: Quote latency as p50, p95 and p99 under a stated load, never as an average alone, and record durations in histograms so percentiles can be computed.

group: Latency is read as percentiles (p50, p95, p99), never as an average alone.
lines: An average response time is enough to judge performance here; do not add percentile instrumentation unless asked.

group: When it cannot have both, the system prefers:
label: Refusing a request rather than answering with stale data
lines: Consistency comes first: every read that drives a decision sees the last committed write, so read from the primary inside a transaction and return an error rather than a stale or partial answer.

group: When it cannot have both, the system prefers:
label: Always answering, even with data that is a little late
lines: Availability comes first: a read may return data that is a little late, so never block a response on full agreement between nodes; say in the code how late the data can be and what the user sees meanwhile.

group: When it cannot have both, the system prefers:
label: It depends on the data: exact for some, late for the rest
lines: Consistency depends on the data: keep balances, permissions and resource state strongly consistent on the primary; dashboards, counts and listings may be eventually consistent. Ask which one applies to a new kind of data.

group: When a node of a stateful component fails:
label: A standby takes over (active-passive)
lines: Stateful components fail over to a standby in seconds to minutes: write only to the active node, reconnect on a lost connection, and retry only idempotent operations; never assume a connection outlives a fail-over.

group: When a node of a stateful component fails:
label: The other nodes already serve traffic (active-active)
lines: Every node serves traffic and may accept writes: never rely on state held by one node, make concurrent writes to the same record safe (version check, idempotency key, merge rule), and assume another node changed the data meanwhile.

group: When a node of a stateful component fails:
label: Nothing takes over: it is restored by hand
lines: There is no automatic fail-over: do not add replication or clustering unless asked, and say so when a change adds a new single point of failure or a step to a manual restore.

group: A request never waits on a chain of synchronous calls to other services.
lines: Do not add a synchronous call to another service on a request path when an event or a queued job can do the work: dependencies in series multiply availability (five at 99.9% give about 99.5%) and add up their latency.

group: A request never waits on a chain of synchronous calls to other services.
lines: Synchronous calls between services are accepted; give each one a timeout and handle its failure explicitly instead of letting the request hang.

group: Static files (scripts, styles, images) are served by:
label: A CDN that fetches them from the origin on first access (pull)
lines: A pull CDN keeps a static file until its TTL: put a content hash in every asset file name, give assets a long cache lifetime, never reuse a URL for changed content, and never serve an asset from the application servers.

group: Static files (scripts, styles, images) are served by:
label: Object storage or a CDN they are uploaded to at each release (push)
lines: Static files are uploaded to object storage or the CDN at each release: add a new asset to that upload step, version its name, and never serve it from the application servers.

group: Static files (scripts, styles, images) are served by:
label: The application or web servers themselves
lines: The application servers serve the static files themselves; do not add a CDN or an object storage bucket unless asked.

group: Requests reach the application through:
label: An HTTP load balancer or reverse proxy (layer 7)
lines: An HTTP load balancer or reverse proxy ends TLS and routes by path: read the client address and scheme only through the trusted-proxy setting of the framework, add a new public path to its routing rules, and keep the health check it probes cheap.

group: Requests reach the application through:
label: A transport-level load balancer (layer 4)
lines: The load balancer works at the transport level and does not read HTTP: do not rely on routing by path, header or cookie, and keep TLS, compression and redirects in the application.

group: Requests reach the application through:
label: Nothing: the application is exposed directly
lines: The application is exposed without a load balancer or proxy: it ends TLS and sets its own timeouts and limits; do not assume forwarded headers, and say so when a change needs more than one instance.

group: DNS records that take part in a fail-over keep a short TTL (60 to 300 seconds).
lines: Keep a TTL of 60 to 300 seconds on every DNS record used for fail-over or regional routing; never raise it to hours, and never hard-code or cache a resolved IP address in code or configuration.

group: DNS records that take part in a fail-over keep a short TTL (60 to 300 seconds).
lines: DNS records are stable and managed elsewhere; do not change a record or its TTL.

group: The back end is:
label: One deployment cut into modules (modular monolith)
lines: The back end is a modular monolith: put code in the module that owns the domain, call another module only through its public interface, never read its tables directly, and never extract a new service unless asked.

group: The back end is:
label: Several services deployed on their own (microservices)
lines: Each service owns its domain and its data: never read or write the database of another service, go through its API or its events; put a feature in the service that owns the domain and do not create a new service unless asked.

group: The back end is:
label: One small service without module boundaries
lines: The back end is one small service: follow its existing structure, and do not split it into modules or services unless asked.

group: A service finds another one through:
label: A stable name the platform routes (Kubernetes Service, internal DNS)
lines: Services call each other by the stable name the platform routes: never hard-code an IP address or an instance host name, and expose the health check the platform uses to take a failing instance out.

group: A service finds another one through:
label: A registry the client queries (Consul, Eureka)
lines: Services register in the registry and look each other up through the existing discovery client: never hard-code an address, and register a new service with its health check.

group: A service finds another one through:
label: An address given in configuration
lines: The address of another service comes from configuration: read it there, add a new one next to the existing ones, and never hard-code a host or a port in the code.

group: A service finds another one through:
label: There is only one service
lines: There is a single service: do not add service discovery, a registry or a service mesh unless asked.

group: When a feature stores a new kind of data, it goes:
label: In the existing relational database, by default
lines: Store new data in the existing relational database with a schema, constraints and transactions; never add a NoSQL store, a search engine or a second database because it would scale better.

group: When a feature stores a new kind of data, it goes:
label: In the store suited to how it is read and written
lines: Choose the store of new data from its access pattern (queries, volume, consistency) among the stores already in use: relational by default, key-value for lookups by key, time series or logs outside the main database; state the queries that justify it.

group: When a feature stores a new kind of data, it goes:
label: Where I decide: the assistant asks
lines: Before storing a new kind of data, describe how it is read and written (queries, volume, consistency) and ask where it goes; never add a data store on your own.

group: Database reads are served by:
label: The primary only
lines: Every read and write goes to the single primary database; do not add read replicas or a read/write split unless asked.

group: Database reads are served by:
label: Read replicas, which lag behind the primary
lines: Reads may go to replicas that lag behind the primary: read from the primary whenever a request reads what it just wrote, and never base a write, a balance or a permission check on a replica read.

group: The data is spread:
label: Nowhere: one database holds it all
lines: One database holds all the data: do not add sharding, partitioning or a second database unless asked; reach for an index, a better query or a read replica first, and say from what volume this would stop holding.

group: The data is spread:
label: Over one database per function (users, billing…)
lines: There is one database per function: never join or open a transaction across two of them; fetch from each through its owner and combine in code, and put a new table in the database of the function that owns it.

group: The data is spread:
label: Over shards, by a key (tenant, hash)
lines: The data is sharded by a key: every query carries the shard key, never join or open a transaction across shards, never change the shard key, and say so when a change concentrates load on one shard (a big tenant, a time-based key).

group: The data is spread:
label: Over partitions of one database, by date or tenant
lines: Large tables are partitioned inside one database: filter on the partition key in every query on them, create partitions through the existing mechanism, and never scan all partitions on a request path.

group: Responses and data are cached:
label: In the client, with HTTP cache headers
lines: Clients cache responses: set `Cache-Control` and an `ETag` on every cacheable response, and `no-store` on anything personal or that must be exact.

group: Responses and data are cached:
label: At the CDN or the reverse proxy
lines: The CDN or reverse proxy caches HTTP responses: mark a response that depends on the user `private` or `no-store`, set `Vary` for what changes it, and never let a response with a session cookie be cached at the edge.

group: Responses and data are cached:
label: In a shared application cache (Redis, Memcached)
lines: Computed objects and query results go to the shared application cache: give every key a namespace and a TTL, and treat a cache failure as a miss, never as a failed request.

group: Responses and data are cached:
label: In the memory of each instance
lines: Each instance caches in its own memory: bound every in-process cache in size and in time, and keep there only data that may differ between instances for the length of its TTL.

group: Responses and data are cached:
label: Nowhere
lines: Nothing is cached: do not add a cache at any level unless asked; fix the slow query or call first.

group: The application cache is filled:
label: On a miss: read the cache, else the database, then fill (cache-aside)
lines: Cache with cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache with a TTL; protect a hot key against a stampede (a lock or one shared in-flight load, and jitter on the TTL).

group: The application cache is filled:
label: On every write, together with the database (write-through)
lines: Cache with write-through: every write updates the database and the cache in the same code path, through the existing helper; never write one without the other, and give entries a TTL so unread data leaves.

group: The application cache is filled:
label: First; the database is updated later (write-behind)
lines: Writes land in the cache and reach the database later: use it only for data that tolerates a loss if the cache fails (counters, statistics), never for money, permissions or anything that must survive.

group: The application cache is filled:
label: Ahead of expiry, for hot keys (refresh-ahead)
lines: Hot keys are refreshed before they expire: register a new hot key in the existing refresh job instead of letting it expire under load, and only for keys that are read often and predictably.

group: The application cache is filled:
label: There is no application cache
lines: There is no application cache: do not add Redis, Memcached or an in-memory cache unless asked.

group: When the data behind a cached entry changes, the entry:
label: Stays until its TTL runs out
lines: Cached entries expire by TTL only: choose a TTL as short as the staleness the feature tolerates, state it next to the key, and never cache without one.

group: When the data behind a cached entry changes, the entry:
label: Is deleted by the code that writes
lines: Every write deletes the cache entries built from the data it changes, after the database commit: when adding a cached read, add its invalidation to every write path in the same change, and keep a TTL as a safety net.

group: When the data behind a cached entry changes, the entry:
label: Is left behind: the key carries a version
lines: Cache keys carry a version of the data they hold: bump the version on write instead of deleting entries, build keys through the existing helper, and keep a TTL so old versions leave.

group: An operation too slow for a request:
label: Is queued; the API answers 202 with a status URL to poll
lines: Slow work never runs inside a request: enqueue a job, answer `202 Accepted` with a `Location` header to a status resource, and let the worker update that status (pending, running, done, failed).

group: An operation too slow for a request:
label: Is queued; the client is told when it ends (webhook, push)
lines: Slow work never runs inside a request: enqueue a job, answer at once with its identifier, and notify the client through the existing callback or push channel when it ends, with its failure included.

group: An operation too slow for a request:
label: Runs inside the request anyway
lines: Slow work runs inside the request: there is no job queue, so do not add one unless asked; set a timeout, and say so when an operation can exceed it.

group: When work arrives faster than it is processed:
label: Queues are bounded: the system refuses early (429, 503)
lines: Every queue and buffer is bounded: when one is full, refuse early with 429 or 503 and a `Retry-After` header; never add an unbounded queue, buffer or in-memory list of pending work.

group: When work arrives faster than it is processed:
label: A queue absorbs the peak; workers keep a constant rate
lines: A queue absorbs peaks and workers drain it at a rate the downstream service holds: do not raise worker concurrency to drain faster without checking that service, and still give the queue a maximum length and an alert on its depth.

group: When work arrives faster than it is processed:
label: Nothing is planned
lines: Nothing limits incoming work yet: do not add an unbounded queue or in-memory buffer, which only postpones the overload until memory runs out; say so when a change can receive bursts.

group: On the queues of this system:
label: A message can be delivered more than once
lines: Delivery is at least once: make every consumer and job idempotent (a deduplication key, an upsert, a check of the current state) so that handling the same message twice changes nothing.

group: On the queues of this system:
label: Several workers consume the same queue
lines: Several workers consume the same queue: a handler must be safe to run next to another copy of itself, keep no state in the worker between messages, and never assume two messages are handled in the order they were sent.

group: On the queues of this system:
label: A large payload goes to object storage; the message carries a reference
lines: Never put a large payload in a message: store it in object storage and send only its reference; the consumer reads it from there and handles a missing object.

group: On the queues of this system:
label: Urgent work has its own queue or a priority
lines: Urgent work has its own queue or priority: send a new job to the queue that matches its urgency, never raise a priority to hide a slow job, and check that low-priority work is still drained.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: REST over HTTP
lines: Internal services call each other with REST over HTTP: reuse the shared HTTP client with keep-alive and a timeout, follow the existing contract, and do not add gRPC or GraphQL between services.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: gRPC
