lines: Internal services call each other with gRPC: change the `.proto` contract first, only by adding fields and never by reusing a field number, regenerate the stubs, and set a deadline on every call; do not add REST calls between services.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: GraphQL
lines: Internal services are reached through GraphQL: extend the existing schema, batch nested lookups to avoid one query per item, and keep the depth and cost limits on queries; do not add another protocol between services.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: Messages only, no direct call
lines: Services exchange messages only: never add a direct synchronous call from one service to another; publish an event or send a command on the existing broker.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: There is only one service
lines: There is a single service: do not add an internal RPC layer or a message broker to split it unless asked.

group: Between internal services, calls use:
label: Something else
lines: Internal services talk with {value}; use it for every call between services and do not introduce another protocol.

group: Clients learn about a change on the server through:
label: Server-Sent Events
lines: Push server changes to clients with Server-Sent Events on the existing stream; do not add WebSocket or polling, and remember that an instance holds each open stream, so events must reach every instance.

group: Clients learn about a change on the server through:
label: WebSocket
lines: Push server changes to clients over the existing WebSocket connection; do not add another channel, handle reconnection, and publish events through the shared broker so every instance can deliver them.

group: Clients learn about a change on the server through:
label: Polling
lines: Clients poll for changes: keep the polled endpoint cheap and cacheable, give it a sensible interval with backoff, and do not add WebSocket or Server-Sent Events unless asked.

group: Clients learn about a change on the server through:
label: Nothing: they reload
lines: There is no real-time channel: do not add WebSocket, Server-Sent Events or polling unless asked.

group: Clients learn about a change on the server through:
label: Something else
lines: Clients learn about server changes through {value}; use it and do not add another real-time channel.

group: A performance change starts from a measurement, never from an intuition about the code.
lines: Before optimising, name the metric that confirms the problem (a latency percentile, queries per request, database CPU), measure it under load, and measure again after the change; never add a cache to hide a chatty or oversized query.

group: A performance change starts from a measurement, never from an intuition about the code.
lines: An obvious inefficiency may be fixed without a measurement; keep the fix small and say what it is expected to improve.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: Many small network or SQL calls per request
lines: Never issue one network or SQL call per item of a list: batch them, join, or fetch with one wider query, and count the calls a request makes when changing a read path.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: Reading more rows or columns than needed
lines: Select only the columns and rows a request uses: project, filter and paginate in the database, never in application code after loading everything.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: A client or a connection pool created per request
lines: Create HTTP clients, database pools and broker connections once and share them; never build one inside a request handler or a job.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: Business logic running inside the database
lines: Keep processing out of the database: no business logic or formatting in stored procedures, triggers or heavy SQL functions; the database stores and queries, the application computes.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: Heavy work on the servers that answer requests
lines: Keep heavy work (reports, image or file processing, bulk updates) off the servers that answer requests: hand it to a background worker through the queue.

group: Under load, this system has to stay clear of:
label: Blocking I/O on a request path
lines: Never block on I/O in a request path: use the asynchronous API of every file, network and database call, and never run a long CPU-bound loop on the thread or event loop that serves requests.

group: Several customers (tenants) share the system:
label: Yes, each with quotas and rate limits
lines: Tenants share the system under quotas: put every new endpoint, job or resource behind the existing per-tenant quota and rate limit, and never let work for one tenant use a pool, a queue or a lock that starves the others.

group: Several customers (tenants) share the system:
label: Yes, without limits per tenant yet
lines: Tenants share the system without limits per tenant: say so when a change lets one tenant consume a shared resource without bound (a list without a page size, a bulk job, a fan-out), and propose a quota rather than adding one unasked.

group: Several customers (tenants) share the system:
label: No
lines: The system serves a single customer: do not add tenant identifiers, per-tenant quotas or tenant isolation unless asked.

group: The health of an instance is checked by:
label: Two probes: liveness and readiness
lines: Liveness answers without calling the database or any other dependency; readiness checks only what the instance needs to take traffic. Never add a dependency check to liveness: a slow database would get every instance restarted.

group: The health of an instance is checked by:
label: One health endpoint
lines: One health endpoint is probed by the load balancer or the orchestrator: keep it fast and free of calls to slow dependencies, and do not add a check that can fail on every instance at once.

group: The health of an instance is checked by:
label: Nothing
lines: No health endpoint exists: do not add one unless asked, and say so when a change needs the platform to know that an instance is ready or stuck.

group: The system is monitored for:
label: Performance: latency, throughput, errors, saturation
lines: Instrument every new endpoint, job and outbound call with the existing metrics and traces: duration, outcome and count, with labels of bounded cardinality (never a user id or a raw URL).

group: The system is monitored for:
label: Availability, measured from outside against an objective (SLO)
lines: Availability is measured by an external probe against an objective: keep the journey it exercises working when changing those endpoints, and say so when a change can spend the error budget (a migration, a restart, a new dependency).

group: The system is monitored for:
label: Security: failed sign-ins, unusual access, audit trail
lines: Emit an audit event through the existing mechanism for every failed sign-in, refused permission and administrative action a change adds, with who, what and when, and no secret in it.

group: The system is monitored for:
label: Usage: who uses what and how much (quotas, billing)
lines: Record usage per account through the existing usage counters for every new feature that is billed or limited by a quota; never derive billing from application logs.

group: The system is monitored for:
label: Nothing yet
lines: There is no monitoring stack yet: do not add metrics, tracing or dashboards unless asked; keep logs useful enough to diagnose a failure.

group: An alert fires on a symptom users feel and leads to one action.
lines: When adding or changing an alert, alert on a symptom users feel (error rate, a latency percentile, availability against its objective), not on a cause; give it one action and a runbook, and never add an alert nobody has to act on.

group: An alert fires on a symptom users feel and leads to one action.
lines: Alerts and dashboards are managed outside this repository; do not add or change one, and say which signal a change would deserve.

group: A workflow that spans several services or steps is driven by:
label: Events: each service reacts to the others (choreography)
lines: Workflows are choreographed: publish an event that states a fact in the past tense and let each service react; carry a correlation id on every event, and propose a coordinator when a flow grows beyond 4 or 5 steps.

group: A workflow that spans several services or steps is driven by:
label: A coordinator that calls each step and tracks the state (orchestration)
lines: Workflows are orchestrated: add a step to the existing coordinator with its state, its retry and its failure path; never let a service trigger the next step on the side with an event or a direct call.

group: A workflow that spans several services or steps is driven by:
label: Nothing: there is no such workflow
lines: There is no workflow across services: do not add a workflow engine, a saga or an event bus unless asked.

group: The order of messages is guaranteed:
label: Per key (partition or message group)
lines: Messages are ordered per key only: give every message about one entity the same partition or group key (its id), never rely on order across keys, and keep handlers fast since a slow message holds back its whole group.

group: The order of messages is guaranteed:
label: Globally, by a single consumer
lines: A single consumer keeps a global order: do not add a second consumer or parallel handling to that queue, and propose ordering per key when throughput becomes the problem.

group: The order of messages is guaranteed:
label: Not at all
lines: Message order is not guaranteed: never write a handler that depends on it; carry a version or a timestamp in the message and ignore one that is older than the state already applied.

group: Messaging also follows:
label: Publish-subscribe: an event is published once for all its subscribers
lines: A fact that interests several consumers is published once on its topic: add a subscriber instead of another direct call from the publisher, never make the publisher know its subscribers, and keep published event shapes backward compatible.

group: Messaging also follows:
label: Pipes and filters: processing in independent stages linked by queues
lines: Processing runs as independent stages linked by queues: add a stage rather than growing an existing one, keep each stage stateless and idempotent, and never share state between stages outside the message.

group: Messaging also follows:
label: A scheduler, agents and a supervisor for long workflows with external systems
lines: Long workflows with external systems go through the scheduler, its agents and the supervisor: add a step with its timeout, retry and compensation, and never call the external system outside an agent.

group: Messaging also follows:
label: None of these
lines: Messaging stays simple here: do not add topics, processing pipelines or a workflow supervisor unless asked.

group: To fit how data is read and written, the system uses:
label: Separate write and read models (CQRS)
lines: Writes go through commands on the write model and reads through the read model, which may be a little late: never write through a read model, never read your own write from it, and keep CQRS out of plain CRUD areas.

group: To fit how data is read and written, the system uses:
label: Event sourcing: the events are the source of truth
lines: State is the projection of an append-only event log: never update or delete a stored event, never change the meaning of an event type; add a new versioned type and keep every old version readable by the projections.

group: To fit how data is read and written, the system uses:
label: Materialized views or precomputed tables
lines: Expensive, frequent reads come from precomputed views: treat a view as late compared with its source, never write to it by hand, update its refresh or projection when the source shape changes, and keep a way to rebuild it from scratch.

group: To fit how data is read and written, the system uses:
label: Index tables kept next to a key-value store
lines: Lookups on a non-key field go through an index table: update every index table in the same write path as the record it points to, and never scan the main store to search by another field.

group: To fit how data is read and written, the system uses:
label: None: one model, read and written
lines: One model is read and written: do not introduce CQRS, event sourcing or materialized views unless asked; on simple CRUD they add complexity without gain.

group: A large upload or download goes:
label: Straight to object storage, with a signed, short-lived URL
lines: Large files move straight between the client and object storage with a pre-signed URL: sign one object path and one operation, valid 15 minutes or less; never sign a whole bucket or a long-lived URL, and never stream the bytes through the API.

group: A large upload or download goes:
label: Through the API
lines: Files go through the API: stream them to storage without buffering a whole file in memory, enforce a size limit at the boundary, and do not hand out direct storage URLs.

group: A large upload or download goes:
label: Nowhere: there is none
lines: The system handles no large file: do not add object storage or an upload path unless asked.

group: In front of the services, there is:
label: An API gateway (routing, TLS, authentication)
lines: An API gateway routes, ends TLS and authenticates: declare a new public route in its configuration, and never put a business rule or a decision in it; it routes and protects, the services decide.

group: In front of the services, there is:
label: A backend per kind of client (backends for frontends)
lines: Each kind of client has its own backend: put aggregation and shaping for a screen in the backend of that client, keep business rules in the services behind, and never copy a rule into two of these backends.

group: In front of the services, there is:
label: A gateway, then a backend per kind of client
lines: A gateway routes and authenticates, then a backend per kind of client aggregates for its screens: keep business rules in the services behind both, never in the gateway and never copied into two client backends.

group: In front of the services, there is:
label: Nothing: clients call the API directly
lines: Clients call the API directly: do not add a gateway or a backend per client unless asked.

group: An older system lives next to this code:
label: Yes, and it is replaced route by route behind a facade (strangler fig)
lines: A legacy system is replaced route by route behind a facade: migrate one route at a time and switch it in the facade, never add a feature to the legacy side, and never propose a rewrite of everything at once.

group: An older system lives next to this code:
label: Yes, and it stays: a translation layer isolates its model
lines: Reach the older or external system only through its translation layer: never let its names, types or status codes leak into the domain model, and map a new field in that layer.

group: An older system lives next to this code:
label: No
lines: There is no legacy system to migrate: change working code in place and in small steps; do not propose a rewrite or add a facade unless asked.

group: Outside the application code, the platform provides:
label: A sidecar or mesh proxy for outgoing calls (retries, TLS, metrics)
lines: A sidecar or mesh proxy handles retries, TLS and metrics of calls between services: do not add retries or TLS for those calls in application code, since two layers of retries multiply the load on a failing service.

group: Outside the application code, the platform provides:
label: A sidecar or agent that ships logs and metrics
lines: A sidecar or agent ships logs and metrics: write logs to standard output and expose metrics the existing way; never add a log shipper, a file appender or a vendor client to the application.

group: Outside the application code, the platform provides:
label: An external configuration store, changed without a deployment
lines: Configuration comes from the external configuration store and can change while the application runs: read a setting through the existing configuration client each time it is needed, never copy it into a constant or a file of the image.

group: Outside the application code, the platform provides:
label: None of these
lines: The platform provides no sidecar or configuration store: configuration is set at deployment, and the application handles its own TLS, retries and log output; do not add a service mesh unless asked.

group: When a call to a dependency fails, the code:
label: Retries with backoff, behind a circuit breaker
lines: Wrap every call to a dependency in the existing retry and circuit breaker: retry only transient errors, with exponential backoff, jitter and a capped number of attempts, and fail fast while the breaker is open.

group: When a call to a dependency fails, the code:
label: Retries with backoff, without a circuit breaker
lines: Retry only transient errors, with exponential backoff, jitter and a small cap on attempts; never retry at once or without limit, and say so when a new call would need a circuit breaker, since retries alone finish off a failing dependency.

group: When a call to a dependency fails, the code:
label: Does not retry: the failure goes back to the caller
lines: Do not retry a failed call to a dependency in code: set a timeout, return the failure to the caller, and do not add a retry loop or a circuit breaker library unless asked.

group: An operation that changes several services or external systems is kept consistent by:
label: Compensating actions that undo the steps already done
lines: Give every step of a workflow across systems a compensating action, run compensations in reverse order when a later step fails, and make each one idempotent; a compensation is not a rollback, since other readers already saw the intermediate state.

group: An operation that changes several services or external systems is kept consistent by:
label: One database transaction: an operation never spans two systems
lines: An operation changes one database inside one transaction: never call another service or an external system inside a transaction, and never split one business operation over two systems without asking.

group: An operation that changes several services or external systems is kept consistent by:
label: Nothing: a failure is repaired by hand
lines: Nothing undoes a workflow that fails half-way: order the steps so the one most likely to fail runs first, log enough to repair by hand, and say so when a change adds a step that can leave data inconsistent.

group: The system also relies on:
label: Separate pools per dependency or per client (bulkheads)
lines: Pools are separated per dependency or per client so a failure stays local: give a new dependency its own bounded connection pool, concurrency limit and timeout, and never route its calls through a pool shared with another one.

group: The system also relies on:
label: A leader elected among the instances for work that runs once
lines: Work that must run once goes through the existing leader election: pass the fencing token (the term number) with every write the leader makes, and never assume the instance is still leader after a pause.

group: The system also relies on:
label: Independent copies of the whole stack, one per group of customers (stamps, cells)
lines: The stack is deployed as independent stamps, each serving a group of customers: never add a call, a shared database or shared state between two stamps, and keep every change deployable one stamp at a time.

group: The system also relies on:
label: Identical back ends in several regions, each able to serve anyone
lines: Any region can serve any user: never keep data or state that exists in one region only, never assume two requests of a user reach the same region, and say how a new kind of data is replicated.

group: The system also relies on:
label: Sign-in delegated to an identity provider (OIDC, SAML)
lines: Sign-in is delegated to an identity provider: never store or check a password here, validate the signature, issuer, audience and expiry of every token, and map provider roles to local permissions in one place.

group: The system also relies on:
label: A dedicated host that validates requests before the trusted services (gatekeeper)
lines: A gatekeeper validates and filters every public request before the trusted services: never expose an internal service around it, keep it free of business logic and of credentials to the data, and still validate inputs in the services.

group: A name says the intent in full words, even when it gets long.
lines: Name every function, variable and type after its intent, in full words (`startInstance(instance)`, not `proc(d, f)`); when a comment is needed to say what a name means, rename instead.

group: A name says the intent in full words, even when it gets long.
lines: Keep names short and follow the abbreviations the code base already uses; do not rename existing identifiers to longer ones as a side effect.

group: I prefer short functions with one responsibility to long ones read top to bottom.
lines: Keep a function to one responsibility, readable on one screen and at a cyclomatic complexity of 10 at most: return early with guard clauses instead of nesting branches.
Do not pass a boolean flag or `null` to switch a function’s behaviour: write two functions or take an options object.

group: I prefer short functions with one responsibility to long ones read top to bottom.
lines: Keep a linear procedure in one function rather than a chain of two-line functions that call each other; extract a function only when it is reused or hides a real detail.

group: When code next to the task deserves a refactor, the assistant:
label: Refactors it in small steps, tests first
lines: Refactor code the task touches in small steps that each keep the tests green; when no test covers it, write the test first, and keep the refactor apart from the behaviour change.

group: When code next to the task deserves a refactor, the assistant:
label: Tells me, and leaves it for a separate change
lines: Do not refactor code next to the task: say what deserves it and why at the end, and leave it for a separate change.

group: When code next to the task deserves a refactor, the assistant:
label: Leaves it alone
lines: Do not refactor or restyle code the task does not require changing, even when it looks improvable.

group: The code is mostly written:
label: With classes and objects
lines: Write new behaviour as methods on the class that owns the data, next to the existing classes; do not add a module of free functions that works on another class’s state.

group: The code is mostly written:
label: With functions and plain data
lines: Write functions over plain data and compose them (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`); do not introduce a class where a function and a type are enough, and share no mutable state between functions.

group: The code is mostly written:
label: Both: objects at the boundaries, functions for calculations
lines: Use objects behind an interface where an implementation can be swapped (providers, storage, plugins), and pure functions over plain data for calculations and transformations.

group: The code is mostly written:
label: Something else
lines: The code is written in this style: {value}; follow it in new code and do not mix in another one.

group: Data is immutable by default: a new value is created rather than changing one in place.
lines: Never mutate an argument or a shared value: return a new one, and declare data read-only (`const`, `readonly`); mutate in place only inside a hot loop where the copy was measured as a cost.

group: Data is immutable by default: a new value is created rather than changing one in place.
lines: Changing a local value in place is fine; never mutate an argument the caller still uses without the function name saying so.

group: Business calculations are pure functions; I/O, the clock and randomness stay at the edges.
lines: Write a business calculation as a pure function of its arguments: read the data before calling it and write the result after, never inside it.
Pass the current time, random values and generated ids in as parameters: a function that reads `Date.now()` or a global is not pure and cannot be tested without a mock.

group: Business calculations are pure functions; I/O, the clock and randomness stay at the edges.
lines: Business code may read the clock and do I/O where it needs it; do not restructure it into pure functions unasked, and keep a way to fake the clock and the I/O in tests.

group: To share behaviour between classes, the code uses:
label: Composition and interfaces, no inheritance of our own
lines: Never extend one of the project’s classes to reuse its code: pass the behaviour in as a collaborator behind an interface. Extending a class the framework requires is fine.

group: To share behaviour between classes, the code uses:
label: Inheritance only for a true “is a” relation
lines: Extend a class only when the subclass can replace its parent everywhere without surprise; to reuse code, compose. Keep hierarchies one level deep.

group: To share behaviour between classes, the code uses:
label: Base classes that hold the common code
lines: Put code shared by sibling classes in their existing base class and leave the steps that differ abstract; do not add a level to the hierarchy unasked.

group: Everything is private unless it has to be public: fields, methods, exports.
lines: Expose the minimum: private fields, no getter or setter added by default, and export only what another module uses; state changes through a method that keeps the object valid.
In TypeScript, `private` is only checked at compile time: use a `#field` when a value must stay private at run time.

group: Everything is private unless it has to be public: fields, methods, exports.
lines: Plain objects with public fields are fine; do not wrap them in classes with getters and setters, and do not narrow existing visibility as a side effect.

group: An abstraction (interface, generic parameter, option) is added:
label: When a second real case exists
lines: Write the concrete code first; add an interface, a generic parameter or an option only when a second real case exists, never for a hypothetical one.

group: An abstraction (interface, generic parameter, option) is added:
label: At the third case
lines: Write the concrete code, and tolerate a second similar case; abstract at the third one, once what really varies is visible.

group: An abstraction (interface, generic parameter, option) is added:
label: Up front, where variation is expected
lines: Where the task names a point that will vary (provider, format, policy), isolate it behind an interface from the start, so that a new case is a new implementation and not an edited `switch`.

group: I prefer a little duplication to the wrong abstraction.
lines: Merge two pieces of code only when they state the same business knowledge and will change for the same reason; code that looks alike by chance stays duplicated.

group: I prefer a little duplication to the wrong abstraction.
lines: Do not repeat logic: before writing a helper, search for an existing one, and extract a shared function as soon as the same logic appears twice.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Single responsibility: one reason to change
lines: Give a class or module one reason to change: do not add billing, notification or another actor’s concern to a service that does something else; create or use the module that owns it.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Open/closed: extend without editing
lines: When a new case would mean editing a `switch` or an `if` chain on a type in several places, add an implementation of the existing interface instead.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Interface segregation: small interfaces per client
lines: Keep an interface to the methods its caller uses: split one that forces an implementation to stub methods, and depend on the narrowest one.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions
lines: Business code depends on an interface it defines, and the detail implements it; this is about the direction of imports, so a dependency injection container alone does not satisfy it.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Law of Demeter: talk to direct neighbours only
lines: Do not chain through an object’s internals (`a.getB().getC().run()`): call a method on the direct collaborator and let it delegate.

group: The assistant holds new code to:
label: Tell, don’t ask
lines: Ask an object to act rather than reading its state to decide in its place: move the condition into a method of the object that owns the data.

group: A design pattern is used only when its problem is really there; a function or a plain object comes first.
lines: Before introducing a design pattern, state the problem it solves here and what it costs; with a single variant, write the direct code.
Prefer a function or an object literal to a Strategy or Factory class hierarchy, and a wrapper function to a Decorator class, when the language allows it.

group: A design pattern is used only when its problem is really there; a function or a plain object comes first.
lines: Use the named patterns the code base already uses (Factory, Builder, Strategy, Adapter, Decorator) and name the classes after them, so that the structure is recognized at a glance.

group: A shared resource (configuration, connection pool, client) reaches the code that uses it:
label: Through constructor or function parameters
lines: Pass a shared resource in through the constructor or the function parameters and create it once at the entry point; never write a Singleton class or reach for a global.

group: A shared resource (configuration, connection pool, client) reaches the code that uses it:
label: Through a dependency injection container
lines: Register a shared resource in the dependency injection container and receive it by injection; never instantiate it inside the class that uses it, and never write a Singleton class.

group: A shared resource (configuration, connection pool, client) reaches the code that uses it:
label: By importing a module-level instance
lines: Import the existing module-level instance of a shared resource; never create a second one, and keep a way to replace it in tests.

group: Source folders are organized:
label: By domain or use case (`billing/`, `instances/`)
lines: Put a new file in the folder of the domain or use case it serves, next to what changes with it; do not create top-level folders named after a technical type (`controllers/`, `utils/`).

group: Source folders are organized:
label: By technical type (`controllers/`, `services/`, `models/`)
lines: Put a new file in the existing folder of its technical type (`controllers/`, `services/`, `models/`) and name it after its domain; do not start a per-domain folder next to them.

group: Source folders are organized:
label: Another way
lines: Source folders are organized this way: {value}; place new files accordingly and do not start another layout.

group: Business code never imports the framework, the ORM or a provider’s client.
lines: Entities and use cases import nothing from the framework, the ORM, HTTP or a provider’s SDK: to reach one, declare an interface in the business code and implement it in an adapter.
Keep business entities apart from ORM models and table shapes, so that the database schema does not dictate the business model.

group: Business code never imports the framework, the ORM or a provider’s client.
lines: Business code may use the framework and the ORM directly; do not add interfaces and mapping layers to hide them, except in front of a detail that is likely to be replaced.

group: A module imports from another module:
label: Only through its public entry point
lines: Import from another module only through its public entry point, never from its internal files; when what you need is not exported, export it there on purpose or ask.

group: A module imports from another module:
label: From any file, as long as there is no cycle
lines: A module may import any file of another one, but never add an import that closes a cycle between two modules.

group: A module imports from another module:
label: No rule
lines: No import rule is enforced between modules; follow the imports the neighbouring files use and avoid adding a dependency between two modules that do not know each other yet.

group: Inside the code base, the structure is:
label: Layers (presentation, application, domain, data)
lines: The code is layered (presentation, application, domain, data): a layer calls only the one below it, never upward or across, and business rules go in the domain layer.
Do not add a layer or a class that only forwards calls to the next one.

group: Inside the code base, the structure is:
label: Hexagonal or clean: a domain core, ports and adapters
lines: The code is hexagonal: dependencies point toward the domain. Use cases declare ports, adapters (controllers, repositories, clients) implement them, and the domain names no outer layer.

group: Inside the code base, the structure is:
label: Feature modules, each with its own internals
lines: The code is split into feature modules: a feature keeps its handlers, logic and data access together; put a change in the module that owns the behaviour and share only through its public interface.

group: Inside the code base, the structure is:
label: The framework’s default (MVC or similar)
lines: The code follows the framework’s default structure: put each file where the framework expects it and do not add layers of your own on top.

group: Inside the code base, the structure is:
label: Something else
lines: The code base is structured this way: {value}; place new code accordingly and do not introduce another structure.

group: When something happens that other parts of the code react to:
label: The code calls them directly
lines: Parts of the code call each other directly, so the flow can be read from the caller; do not introduce an event bus, an emitter or an observer unasked.

group: When something happens that other parts of the code react to:
label: It publishes an event that subscribers handle
lines: Publish an event named in the past tense for a fact others react to, and add a subscriber instead of a direct call; the publisher never knows its subscribers.
Write every event handler so that a duplicate or out-of-order event does no harm, carry a correlation id on each event and log it, and unsubscribe what you subscribe.

group: The code base uses:
label: CQRS: separate read and write models
lines: Reads and writes use separate models: a command changes state through the write model and returns no data, a query reads the read model and changes nothing; expect the read side to lag.

group: The code base uses:
label: Event sourcing: state rebuilt from stored events
lines: State is rebuilt from stored events: never edit or delete a stored event, change state only by appending one, and give a changed event shape a new version that old events are upgraded to.

group: The code base uses:
label: A small core extended by plugins
lines: Add a feature as a plugin against the existing plugin contract, not in the core; treat that contract as public and never change it without asking.

group: The code base uses:
label: Functions run on demand (serverless)
lines: Handlers run as on-demand functions: keep them short and stateless between calls, do the expensive setup outside the handler, and move work that may exceed the time limit elsewhere.

group: The code base uses:
label: None of these
lines: Do not introduce CQRS, event sourcing, a plugin system or on-demand functions unasked: one model serves reads and writes, and state is stored as it is.

group: The logic of a business action lives in:
label: One use case per action (`StartInstance`)
lines: Write each business action as its own use case that loads, calls the domain and saves, testable without the framework; a controller only validates, calls it and translates the result.

group: The logic of a business action lives in:
label: A service per resource (`InstanceService`)
lines: Put the logic of a business action in a method of the service that owns the resource; a controller only validates, calls it and translates the result into a response.

group: The logic of a business action lives in:
label: The handler itself, one procedure per action
lines: Write a business action as one procedure in its handler that reads, decides and writes; move a rule to a shared function once a second handler needs it, never copy it.

group: Domain-Driven Design building blocks (entities, value objects, aggregates) are used:
label: In the complex core of the business only
lines: Model the complex core of the business with entities, value objects and aggregates; write simple create-read-update-delete and configuration code plainly, without them.
Make a value object immutable and compared by value, validated when built (`Money`, `Region`); an entity is compared by identity.

group: Domain-Driven Design building blocks (entities, value objects, aggregates) are used:
label: Everywhere
lines: Model every business concept as an entity (has an identity) or a value object (defined by its values), and change an aggregate only through its root, one aggregate per transaction.
Make a value object immutable and compared by value, validated when built (`Money`, `Region`); an entity is compared by identity.

group: Domain-Driven Design building blocks (entities, value objects, aggregates) are used:
label: Not used
lines: Do not introduce Domain-Driven Design building blocks (aggregates, value object classes, domain events) unasked: follow the data structures the code already uses.

group: A business object carries its own rules and refuses an invalid change itself.
lines: Put a business rule in a method of the entity it protects (`instance.stop(now)` throws on a forbidden transition); never set a status or a field from outside and never add a public setter for it.

group: A business object carries its own rules and refuses an invalid change itself.
lines: Entities are plain data and the rules live in services: put a rule in the service that owns the action, in one place, and do not add behaviour to the data types.

group: The code uses the words of the business: when a concept is renamed, the code is renamed.
lines: Name types, functions and tables with the exact words the business uses, one word per concept and no synonym; when a term in the task matches no name in the code, ask instead of inventing one.
The same word can mean different things in two contexts (an instance for provisioning, an instance for billing): keep one model per context and translate between them, never share one type.

group: The code uses the words of the business: when a concept is renamed, the code is renamed.
lines: Keep the names the code already has, even when the business now uses another word; do not rename identifiers to follow vocabulary unasked.

group: Business code loads and saves its objects through:
label: Repositories that hide the ORM or the SQL
lines: Load and save business objects through a repository (`findById`, `save`) that returns domain objects, never ORM rows or query builders; add the method you need to the existing repository.

group: Business code loads and saves its objects through:
label: Models that save themselves (Active Record)
lines: Models load and save themselves: use their own query and save methods and do not wrap them in repository classes.

group: Business code loads and saves its objects through:
label: The ORM or database client, called directly
lines: Call the ORM or the database client directly where the data is needed; do not add a repository layer that only forwards to it.

group: What crosses the API is a dedicated shape, never a database model or an entity as is.
lines: Never return or accept a database model or an entity as is: map it to a flat transfer shape that lists each exposed field, so that an internal field never leaks and a schema change never changes the contract.

group: What crosses the API is a dedicated shape, never a database model or an entity as is.
lines: Models may be returned as they are, without a mapping layer; before exposing one, check that it holds no internal or sensitive field and hide those explicitly.

group: A method either changes state or returns a value, never both.
lines: Write a method as a command that changes state and returns nothing beyond an id or a status, or as a query that returns a value and changes nothing; a `get…` or `find…` never writes.

group: A method either changes state or returns a value, never both.
lines: A method may change state and return the result; still, never hide a write behind a name that reads (`get…`, `find…`, `is…`).

group: A rule, a regular expression or a database query is preferred to a model call whenever it does the job.
lines: Before adding a model call, check whether a rule, a regular expression or a database query does the job; call a model only where they cannot, and say why in the change.

group: A rule, a regular expression or a database query is preferred to a model call whenever it does the job.
lines: A model call is acceptable where it saves code; still use deterministic code for anything with one exact answer (parsing, arithmetic, lookups, permission checks).

group: A new model feature starts with a success criterion and evaluation cases, before its prompt.
lines: Before writing the prompt of a new model feature, write down the task, its success criterion and a first set of evaluation cases; a prompt that works on three examples proves nothing.

group: A new model feature starts with a success criterion and evaluation cases, before its prompt.
lines: A new model feature may start as a prototype (model and prompt); add evaluation cases before it reaches users, and say when a feature has none.

group: Before a call, the size of the input in tokens is:
label: Counted with the tokenizer and checked against a budget
lines: Count the input tokens of a call with the tokenizer helper the project uses and compare them to the budget of that call before sending; trim or refuse an input that exceeds it instead of letting the provider reject it.

group: Before a call, the size of the input in tokens is:
label: Estimated from the character count
lines: Estimate the input size of a call at about 4 characters per token (fewer for non-English text) and keep a margin under the context window, which holds the prompt and the answer together.

group: Before a call, the size of the input in tokens is:
label: Not checked
lines: Input size is not checked before a call: bound every user-supplied text with a maximum length, and handle the context-length error of the provider as an expected case.

group: What the model remembers from one call to the next comes from:
label: A conversation stored on our server
lines: The conversation is stored on the server: rebuild the messages of each call from that store, scoped to the signed-in user, and never accept system instructions or past assistant turns from the client.

group: What the model remembers from one call to the next comes from:
label: The history the client sends with each request
lines: The client sends the history with each request: treat all of it as untrusted input, validate its roles and size, and add the system instructions on the server only.

group: What the model remembers from one call to the next comes from:
label: Nothing: each call stands alone
lines: Each model call stands alone: put everything the call needs in its own input, and do not add conversation storage unasked.

group: Model identifiers are written:
label: In one configuration module, by task
lines: Model identifiers live in one configuration module, keyed by task: reference that entry at the call site and never write a model identifier as a string literal anywhere else.

group: Model identifiers are written:
label: In environment variables
lines: Model identifiers come from environment variables: read them through the configuration layer, document a new variable in the example environment file, and never hard-code a model identifier.

group: Model identifiers are written:
label: Next to each call
lines: Model identifiers are written next to each call, as a named constant: keep the exact, dated identifier and do not use a floating alias that changes model without a code change.

group: Model identifiers are written:
label: Somewhere else
lines: Model identifiers are configured here: {value}; never write one anywhere else.

group: Code that needs a model calls:
label: Our own interface, which hides the provider
lines: Call a model only through the project interface that hides the provider: never import the SDK of a provider outside the module that implements it, and keep provider-specific types out of feature code.

group: Code that needs a model calls:
label: A provider-agnostic library
lines: Call a model through the provider-agnostic library the project already uses; do not import the SDK of a provider directly, and do not rely on an option only one provider supports without saying so.

group: Code that needs a model calls:
label: The provider’s SDK directly
lines: The project calls the SDK of the model provider directly: keep those calls in the existing client module, and do not add a second provider or an abstraction layer unasked.

group: Which model handles a task:
label: One model for everything
lines: One model serves every task: use the configured one for a new call and do not introduce a second model unasked.

group: Which model handles a task:
label: A model chosen per task (small, large, reasoning)
lines: Each task has its own model: for a new task, pick the smallest configured model that passes its evaluation cases, and keep a reasoning model for hard multi-step tasks since it is slower and costs more.

group: Which model handles a task:
label: A small model by default, a larger one for hard cases
lines: Send a task to the small default model first and escalate to the larger one only through the existing routing rule; never call the larger model directly from feature code.

group: Sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, penalties) are set:
label: Per task, in configuration next to the model
lines: Sampling parameters are set per task in configuration, next to the model: add or change them there, never inline at a call site.

group: Sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, penalties) are set:
label: At each call
lines: Set sampling parameters explicitly at each call: temperature 0 to 0.2 for extraction, classification, JSON, code and SQL; 0.5 to 0.8 for conversation; higher only for drafting and ideas.

group: Sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, penalties) are set:
label: Nowhere: the provider’s defaults apply
lines: Leave sampling parameters at the defaults of the provider; when a task needs a predictable output, say so and propose a temperature instead of setting one silently.

group: Every call sets a maximum output length and checks why the model stopped.
lines: Set an explicit maximum output length on every model call, sized for the task, and check the stop reason: an answer cut by the limit is an error to handle, never a JSON document to parse or a text to show as complete.

group: Every call sets a maximum output length and checks why the model stopped.
lines: Leave the output length at its default unless the provider requires one; still check the stop reason before parsing a structured answer, since a truncated one is invalid.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: PostgreSQL with pgvector
lines: Embeddings live in PostgreSQL with pgvector: add a vector column through a migration with its approximate index (HNSW or IVFFlat), and combine similarity with ordinary SQL filters and joins in one query; do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: Qdrant
lines: Embeddings live in Qdrant: reach it through the existing client module, store the filterable fields in the payload with their indexes, and do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: Weaviate
lines: Embeddings live in Weaviate: reach it through the existing client module, declare a new property in the collection schema before using it as a filter, and do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: Chroma
lines: Embeddings live in Chroma: reach it through the existing client module, store filterable fields as metadata, and do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: LanceDB
lines: Embeddings live in LanceDB: reach it through the existing module, keep filterable fields as columns of the table, and do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: An in-memory FAISS index
lines: Embeddings are searched in an in-memory FAISS index, which is a library and not a database: keep the code that rebuilds and persists it working, and keep the mapping from vector position to record and its metadata in the main database.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: A managed vector database service
lines: Embeddings live in a managed vector database service: reach it through the existing client module, send it only the metadata needed for filtering, and do not add another vector store.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: Nowhere: no embeddings
lines: The project stores no embeddings: do not add an embedding model, a vector column or a vector store unasked.

group: Embeddings are stored in:
label: Something else
lines: Embeddings are stored in {value}; reach it through the existing module and do not add another vector store.

group: To change the embedding model or its dimension, the assistant:
label: Asks me first
lines: Ask before changing the embedding model or its dimension: every stored vector has to be computed again, so say how many records that is.

group: To change the embedding model or its dimension, the assistant:
label: May do it, with a full re-index in the same change
lines: A change of embedding model or dimension ships with the job that computes every stored vector again and the switch to the new index; never leave vectors from two models in one searchable index.

group: What a search over embeddings may return is limited:
label: By customer or user: access rights apply
lines: Every search over embeddings carries the tenant and access-right filter inside the query itself, taken from the authenticated session and never from the model or the request text; a search without it is a bug, and so is a test that does not cover two tenants.

group: What a search over embeddings may return is limited:
label: By metadata only (product, language, date)
lines: Apply metadata filters (product, language, date) inside the search query, never on its results: filtering afterwards can leave none of the top results.

group: What a search over embeddings may return is limited:
label: Not at all: one corpus everyone may read
lines: The indexed corpus is readable by every user: never index a private or per-customer document into it, and stop and ask when a new source holds some.

group: To give the model passages of our data (RAG), the project retrieves them with:
label: Vector search only
lines: Retrieval is vector search only: keep the number of passages a named setting (5 to 20 in practice), and say when a query depends on exact terms (codes, names, identifiers) that vector search misses.

group: To give the model passages of our data (RAG), the project retrieves them with:
label: Hybrid search (vectors and keywords)
lines: Retrieval is hybrid: run the vector and the keyword (BM25) search and merge them through the existing function; never drop the keyword side, which finds exact codes, names and identifiers.

group: To give the model passages of our data (RAG), the project retrieves them with:
label: Hybrid search, then re-ranking
lines: Retrieval is hybrid search then re-ranking: fetch a wide candidate set (about 20), re-rank it, and pass only the best (about 5) to the model; keep both numbers named settings.

group: To give the model passages of our data (RAG), the project retrieves them with:
label: No retrieval: the whole corpus fits in the context
lines: The whole corpus is sent in the context, with no retrieval: keep it small and stable, place it in the cached prefix, and say when it grows past what one call should carry.

group: To give the model passages of our data (RAG), the project retrieves them with:
label: Not used
lines: The project does not use retrieval-augmented generation: do not add a retrieval step, an index or a vector store unasked.

group: Before indexing, documents are split:
label: Along their structure (headings, paragraphs)
lines: Split documents along their structure (headings, paragraphs, list items) into passages of about 200 to 800 tokens, never in the middle of a sentence, a table or a code block.

group: Before indexing, documents are split:
label: Into fixed-size passages with an overlap
lines: Split documents into fixed-size passages (about 200 to 800 tokens) with a 10 to 20 % overlap; keep the size and the overlap named settings, and re-index when either changes.

group: Before indexing, documents are split:
label: Not at all: one vector per document
lines: Each document is indexed whole, as one vector: keep documents short enough for the embedding model, and do not add a splitting step unasked.

group: Before indexing, documents are split:
label: Another way
lines: Documents are split this way before indexing: {value}; follow it for a new source.

group: An answer built from retrieved passages uses only them, cites its sources, and says when the information is missing.
lines: A prompt that receives retrieved passages tells the model to answer from them only, to return the identifiers of the passages used, and to say so when they do not hold the answer; check in code that every returned source was among the passages sent.

group: An answer built from retrieved passages uses only them, cites its sources, and says when the information is missing.
lines: A model may complete retrieved passages with its general knowledge; keep the output able to tell which statements come from a source, and never invent a source reference.

group: Prompts live:
label: In their own files, in one folder of the repository
lines: Prompts live in their own files in the prompts folder of the repository: add a new prompt there, load it through the existing loader, and never write prompt text inline in feature code.

group: Prompts live:
label: In the code, next to the call that uses them
lines: A prompt lives next to the call that uses it, as a named constant or a function that builds it; never assemble one from string pieces scattered across modules.

group: Prompts live:
label: In a prompt management tool, outside the repository
lines: Prompts live in a prompt management tool outside the repository: fetch one by name and pinned version, never copy its text into the code, and say which prompt and version a change expects.

group: Prompts live:
label: Somewhere else
lines: Prompts live here: {value}; add and change them there only.

group: A prompt in this project always:
label: Wraps data in delimiters, apart from the instructions
lines: In a prompt, keep instructions in the system part and wrap every piece of data (user text, documents, tool results) in named delimiters such as `<docs>` and `<question>`; never concatenate user text into the instructions.

group: A prompt in this project always:
label: States the role, what to refuse and when to say “I do not know”
lines: Start a system prompt with the role of the model, what it does, what it refuses, and the instruction to say so when the information is missing.

group: A prompt in this project always:
label: States the output format
lines: State the expected output format in every prompt (fields, types, language, length) and keep it in step with the schema the code validates the answer against.

group: A prompt in this project always:
label: Gives a few input and output examples
lines: Give a prompt a few varied input and output examples when the format or the tone is precise; keep them few, since they cost tokens and the model copies them too closely.

group: A prompt in this project always:
label: Asks for step-by-step reasoning before the answer
lines: Ask for step-by-step reasoning before the final answer on calculation, logic and multi-step decisions, in a field apart from the answer; leave it out for a reasoning model, which already does it, and for simple tasks.

group: To change an existing prompt, the assistant:
label: Asks me first
lines: Ask before changing an existing prompt, with the proposed wording and the case it fixes: a retouch that fixes one case often breaks others.

group: To change an existing prompt, the assistant:
label: May do it, and replays the evaluation cases
lines: An existing prompt may be changed when its evaluation cases are replayed before and after; report both results, and add a case for the behaviour the change is meant to fix.

group: To change an existing prompt, the assistant:
label: Never does
lines: Never change the text of an existing prompt: describe the change you would make and the case it fixes, and leave the edit to the owner.

group: A call receives only what it needs: more context is not better.
lines: Send a call only what its task needs: select documents and fields instead of passing whole records, date or drop outdated and contradictory sources, and justify any growth of the context with an evaluation result.

group: A call receives only what it needs: more context is not better.
lines: Passing generous context is accepted where it stays well under the window; still remove contradictory or outdated sources, since the model cannot tell which one is right.

group: The fixed part of the context comes first and stays identical between calls, so that prompt caching applies.
lines: Build the context in a stable order: fixed instructions and tool definitions first, byte-identical between calls, then documents, history and the current message; never put a date, an identifier or a per-user value in the fixed prefix.

group: The fixed part of the context comes first and stays identical between calls, so that prompt caching applies.
lines: The project does not rely on prompt caching: order the context for clarity, and do not add cache markers or reorder a prompt for caching unasked.

group: When a conversation or its inputs grow long, the project:
label: Summarizes the older turns
lines: When the history nears its token budget, replace the older turns with a summary through the existing compaction step; keep the system instructions and the latest turns verbatim, and store the summary rather than computing it again at each call.

group: When a conversation or its inputs grow long, the project:
label: Drops the oldest turns
lines: When the history nears its token budget, drop the oldest turns first, never the system instructions, and never cut between a request and the answer that goes with it.

group: When a conversation or its inputs grow long, the project:
label: Refuses past a limit and asks to start again
lines: Past the configured length, refuse the request with a clear message asking to start a new conversation; never trim or summarize a conversation silently.

group: When a conversation or its inputs grow long, the project:
label: Has no long conversation
lines: Calls are short and single-purpose: do not add history trimming or summarizing unasked, and bound the size of each input instead.

group: An answer shown to a user is:
label: Streamed as it is generated (server-sent events)
lines: Stream an answer shown to a user as server-sent events through the existing streaming helper: handle an error and a client disconnect in the middle of the stream, cancel the provider call when the client leaves, and validate or store the text only once it is complete.

group: An answer shown to a user is:
label: Sent once complete
lines: Model answers are returned once complete: do not add streaming unasked, and give the request a timeout that fits the longest expected answer.

group: An answer shown to a user is:
label: Produced by a background job, never during a request
lines: Call a model from a background job only, never inside a request handler: the request enqueues the job and the client reads the result later; make the job safe to retry.

group: Every call to a model has:
label: A timeout
lines: Give every model call an explicit timeout and pass the cancellation signal of the request down to it; never rely on the default of the SDK.

group: Every call to a model has:
label: Retries with backoff on rate limits and server errors
lines: Retry a model call only on a rate limit (429), a server error (5xx) or a network failure, with exponential backoff, jitter and a small maximum; never retry another 4xx, and do not stack your own retries on those of the SDK.

group: Every call to a model has:
label: A fallback model
lines: When the main model stays unavailable after its retries, fall back to the configured fallback model through the existing helper, and record which model answered.

group: Every call to a model has:
label: A quota per user or customer
lines: Check the token or request quota of the user or the customer before a model call and record the usage after it; a new feature that calls a model goes through the same quota.

group: Every call to a model has:
label: A way for the feature to work without the model
lines: A feature that calls a model keeps working when the model does not answer: return the designed fallback (a plain result, a clear message), never an unhandled error or an endless spinner.

group: When code reads a model answer, the answer is:
label: Constrained to a schema by the provider, then validated
lines: When code reads a model answer, request structured output with a schema defined once in the validation library of the project, derive the type from it, and still validate the parsed answer before use.

group: When code reads a model answer, the answer is:
label: JSON asked for in the prompt, then validated
lines: When code reads a model answer, ask for JSON in the prompt, parse it and validate it against a schema; on a failure, retry a bounded number of times with the validation error, then fail clearly.

group: When code reads a model answer, the answer is:
label: Free text: code never reads it
lines: Model answers are free text shown to people: never parse one with a regular expression or branch on its wording; when code needs a value from the model, stop and ask.

group: With the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the product:
label: Exposes an MCP server to its users’ tools
lines: The product exposes an MCP server: build it on the official MCP SDK, give each tool a typed argument schema and a description written for a model, and treat tool names and arguments as a public contract that does not change shape once released.

group: With the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the product:
label: Connects to MCP servers as a client
lines: The product connects to MCP servers as a client: connect only to the servers listed in configuration, treat tool descriptions and results as untrusted data, and never forward the credentials of a user to a server.

group: With the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the product:
label: Does both
lines: The product exposes an MCP server and connects to others: build both on the official MCP SDK, keep released tool names and arguments stable, connect only to configured servers, and treat what they return as untrusted data.

group: With the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the product:
label: Does not use it
lines: The product does not use the Model Context Protocol: do not add an MCP server or client unasked.

group: The MCP server the product exposes is reached:
label: Over HTTP, by authenticated users
lines: The MCP server is remote, over Streamable HTTP: authenticate every request, check the scope of the token and the ownership of the resource in each tool, log each tool call, and add a tool that writes only with its own scope: each tool is attack surface.

group: The MCP server the product exposes is reached:
label: As a local process (stdio)
lines: The MCP server runs as a local process over stdio: write protocol messages only to standard output and logs to standard error, and read credentials from the environment, never from tool arguments.

group: The MCP server the product exposes is reached:
label: There is none
lines: The product exposes no MCP server: do not add an MCP endpoint or transport unasked.

group: In production, models run:
label: At a model provider, through its API
lines: Models are hosted by a model provider: keep its API key on the server, never in client code or in a prompt, and do not add a self-hosted model or an inference server unasked.

group: In production, models run:
label: On our own servers (open-weight models)
lines: Models are self-hosted open-weight models behind an inference server: keep the model, its quantization, the maximum context length and the concurrency limit in configuration, and remember that long contexts and concurrent requests are what fill GPU memory.

group: In production, models run:
label: Both
lines: Some tasks run on a hosted model and some on a self-hosted one: follow the existing assignment for a new task, and never send to the hosted model the data that the self-hosted one exists to keep in house.

group: In production, models run:
label: On the user’s device (browser or app)
lines: Models run on the device of the user: keep them small, load them lazily with a visible progress state, and provide a path for a device that cannot run them.

group: In automated tests, a call to a model is:
label: Replaced by a fake or a recorded answer
lines: Automated tests never call a model: swap the model client for the existing fake or a recorded answer, and test the code around the call (prompt building, parsing, validation, error paths, truncated and malformed answers).

group: In automated tests, a call to a model is:
label: Sent to a small model running locally
lines: Automated tests call a small local model through the same interface as production: assert on structure and invariants, never on exact wording, and do not judge answer quality from it.

group: In automated tests, a call to a model is:
label: Sent to the real model, with a test key
lines: Tests that call the real model are kept apart from unit tests, few and tagged so they can be skipped: assert on structure and invariants, never on exact wording, and cap what one run may spend.

group: Fine-tuning:
label: Is not used
lines: The project does not fine-tune models: improve a result through the prompt, the context or retrieval, and do not propose fine-tuning or add training code unasked.

group: Fine-tuning:
label: Is used, with adapters (LoRA) loaded at deployment
lines: Fine-tuning produces adapters loaded at deployment: version an adapter with the exact base model and the dataset it came from, never commit weights to the repository, and replay the evaluation set before one replaces another.

group: Fine-tuning:
label: Is used, and produces whole models
lines: Fine-tuning produces whole models: version each with the dataset and the settings it came from, never commit weights to the repository, and replay the evaluation set before one replaces another.

group: Evaluation cases for model features are run with:
label: Our own scripts or the project’s test runner
lines: Evaluation cases are files in the repository (input, expected result, category) run by the existing evaluation script: add cases there, and report scores per category rather than one global number.

group: Evaluation cases for model features are run with:
label: DeepEval
lines: Evaluations run with DeepEval: write a new one as a test case next to the existing ones, with the metrics the project already uses, and do not add another evaluation framework.

group: Evaluation cases for model features are run with:
label: Ragas
lines: Evaluations run with Ragas: reuse its faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and context recall metrics, and do not add another evaluation framework.

group: Evaluation cases for model features are run with:
label: Nothing: there are none yet
lines: The project has no evaluation set yet: say so whenever a change touches a prompt, a model or retrieval, and propose the first cases instead of claiming the change is an improvement.

group: Evaluation cases for model features are run with:
label: Something else
lines: Evaluations run with {value}; add new cases there and do not add another evaluation framework.

group: Model outputs are scored by:
label: Deterministic checks (valid JSON, exact value, forbidden word)
lines: Score with a deterministic check whatever has a right answer (valid JSON, exact value, expected call, forbidden word absent); do not use a model as a judge where a rule decides.

group: Model outputs are scored by:
label: A model that grades against a rubric
lines: A model used as a judge grades against a written rubric with explicit criteria, at low temperature, with a structured verdict; never change its prompt or its model without comparing its grades again with human ones, and beware its bias toward long answers.

group: Model outputs are scored by:
label: People who review samples
lines: People review samples of model outputs: keep producing the export they review when an output format changes, and flag for review the cases where automatic scores and the expected result disagree.

group: Model outputs are scored by:
label: Retrieval metrics, apart from the answer
lines: Evaluate retrieval apart from generation: each retrieval case names the passages that should be found, and a wrong answer is first checked for a missed passage before the prompt is touched.

group: A change to a prompt, a model or retrieval is checked against the evaluation cases:
label: In CI, which blocks under a threshold
lines: CI replays the evaluation cases on any change to a prompt, a model, sampling parameters or retrieval and blocks under the threshold: never lower the threshold, skip the job or remove a case to get a change through.

group: A change to a prompt, a model or retrieval is checked against the evaluation cases:
label: By hand, before the change is merged
lines: Before handing back a change to a prompt, a model, sampling parameters or retrieval, run the evaluation command and report the scores before and after; when you cannot run it, say so.

group: A change to a prompt, a model or retrieval is checked against the evaluation cases:
label: Not systematically
lines: No evaluation run gates a change: state in the summary of any change to a prompt, a model or retrieval that it is unmeasured, and list the cases you tried by hand.

group: Model calls are traced with:
label: OpenTelemetry
lines: Trace model calls with OpenTelemetry: wrap each retrieval, model call and tool execution in a span under the trace of the request, with the model, token counts, duration and stop reason as attributes.

group: Model calls are traced with:
label: Langfuse
lines: Trace model calls with Langfuse through the existing wrapper: every new call goes through it, named after its feature and linked to the trace of the request; do not add another tracing tool.

group: Model calls are traced with:
label: The application’s structured logs
lines: Log one structured event per model call through the logger of the project: feature, model, token counts, duration, stop reason and the request identifier.

group: Model calls are traced with:
label: Nothing
lines: Model calls are not traced: do not add a tracing tool unasked, but keep the request identifier, the model and the stop reason in the error raised when a call fails.

group: Model calls are traced with:
label: Something else
lines: Model calls are traced with {value}; send every new call through it and do not add another tracing tool.

group: In logs and traces, the content of prompts and answers is:
label: Never kept: metadata only
lines: Never write the content of a prompt or of a model answer to a log, a trace or an error message: record metadata only (feature, model, token counts, duration, stop reason, identifiers).

group: In logs and traces, the content of prompts and answers is:
label: Kept with personal data and secrets masked
lines: Prompts and answers are stored only after the existing masking step has removed personal data and secrets; never log them through another path, and keep their retention limited.

group: In logs and traces, the content of prompts and answers is:
label: Kept in full
lines: Prompts and answers are stored in full in the tracing store only, never in application logs or error messages; say when a new feature would put personal data or secrets into them.

group: Every model call records its token usage, attributed to a feature and a customer.
lines: Record for every model call the input, output and cached token counts returned by the provider, with the model, the feature and the customer; a new call that is not attributed is incomplete, and prices live in one table, never in feature code.

group: Every model call records its token usage, attributed to a feature and a customer.
lines: Token usage is not tracked per call: do not add usage tables or cost dashboards unasked, but say when a change multiplies the number or the size of model calls.

group: Any text the model reads may be hostile: safety comes from permissions and validation outside the model, never from the system prompt.
lines: Treat every text a model reads (user message, document, web page, file, image, transcript) as able to carry instructions: never rely on a prompt to enforce a rule, enforce permissions and limits in code, and keep secrets and other users’ data out of the context.

group: Any text the model reads may be hostile: safety comes from permissions and validation outside the model, never from the system prompt.
lines: The model only reads content written by trusted staff: delimit it all the same, never place a key or a token in a prompt, and say when a change lets outside content reach a model.

group: Personal or confidential data sent to an outside model provider:
label: Never leaves our systems
lines: Never put personal or confidential data in a call to an outside model provider; when a feature needs it, stop and ask instead of sending it.

group: Personal or confidential data sent to an outside model provider:
label: Is masked or pseudonymized first
lines: Before a call to an outside model provider, pass the input through the existing masking step and restore the values in the answer afterwards; a new call that skips it is a bug.

group: Personal or confidential data sent to an outside model provider:
label: Is allowed, under our contract with the provider
lines: Personal data may be sent to the model provider under the existing contract: send the minimum fields the task needs, never a whole record, and keep the configured region and retention settings untouched.

group: Personal or confidential data sent to an outside model provider:
label: No outside provider is used
lines: No data goes to an outside model provider: do not add a call to a hosted model, a hosted embedding service or a hosted moderation service unasked.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Size limits on what users send
lines: Validate the size and the type of everything a user can send to a model (text length, file size, number of files, image or audio duration) at the boundary, before any token is spent.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Moderation of inputs
lines: Pass user input through the existing moderation step before the model call; a new entry point that reaches a model goes through it too, and a refused input gets a clear message, not an error.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Moderation of outputs
lines: Pass a model answer through the existing moderation step before a user sees it or it is stored; with streaming, hold or cut the stream as that step requires.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Model output shown as text, never run or rendered as HTML
lines: Show model output as text: escape it like any user content, render Markdown through the sanitizing renderer only, and never evaluate it, run it as a command or follow a link it holds automatically.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Adversarial test cases (injection attempts)
lines: When a feature lets new content reach a model, add adversarial cases to the evaluation set (instructions hidden in a document, attempts to reveal the system prompt or other users’ data) and keep them passing.

group: Around a model call that serves users, the project has:
label: Test cases that compare answers across user profiles
lines: When a prompt decides or ranks something about people, add evaluation cases that vary only the profile of the user and check the answers stay equivalent; document the known limits next to the prompt.

group: When the steps are known in advance, we write a fixed workflow in code rather than an agent.
lines: When the steps of a task are known in advance, write them as a fixed workflow in code (model calls chained in a set order); let the model choose the next action only where the path truly depends on what it observes, and say why.

group: When the steps are known in advance, we write a fixed workflow in code rather than an agent.
lines: New model-driven features are built as agents on the existing loop, even when the steps look predictable; still give each one its tools, its limits and its logs.

group: The agent is built as:
label: One agent in a reason-act-observe loop
lines: The agent is one model in a reason-act-observe loop: add a capability as a tool of that loop, and do not introduce a planner, a critic or a second agent without asking.

group: The agent is built as:
label: A planner that writes the plan, an executor that runs each step
lines: The agent is a planner and an executor: the planner writes the full list of steps, the executor runs one step at a time with tools, and a failed step goes back to the planner to re-plan rather than being forced through.

group: The agent is built as:
label: An orchestrator and specialised worker agents
lines: The agent is an orchestrator with specialised workers: give each worker its own narrow prompt, tools and context, pass it only what its subtask needs, and return a short result to the orchestrator; ask before adding a new worker.

group: The agent is built as:
label: A graph of steps with explicit dependencies
lines: The agent is a graph of steps: add a step as a node with explicit inputs, outputs and dependencies, run independent branches in parallel, and keep each node resumable after a failure.

group: The agent is built as:
label: Something else
lines: The agent follows this architecture: {value}. Extend it in the same shape and ask before introducing another pattern.

group: A planner, a critic or one more agent is added only when a measure on a task set shows the simpler design fails.
